subsubtopic: STUDY OF EFFECT OF FREON GAS ON OZONE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas the threat of depletion of the earth's protective layer of ozone arising from the freon gas contained in aerosol cans has become so serious as to be the subject of studies in the scientific journal Nature and to cause others to warn that life on earth will be threatened within 10 to 15 years if present production of freon gas continues, I move:
That this matter be directed to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry for immediate consideration to determine whether sufficient funds and personnel are available to the atmospheric processes research branch to make effective studies and to return reports in the shortest possible time.

subsubtopic: STUDY OF EFFECT OF FREON GAS ON OZONE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STUDY OF EFFECT OF FREON GAS ON OZONE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext: Order. I regret to intervene at this point in connection with a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43, but since a motion requires unanimous consent there is often a temptation to believe that it is not necessary for hon. members to comply rigidly with the rule. I would point out, however, that Standing Order 43, in a similar way to Standing Order 26, requires that the subject matter presented pursuant to the rule should be a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The motion proposed relates to a problem which has certainly been with us for some time; if the situation becomes more serious it may have terrible implications 10 or 15 years from now. However, in present circumstances I must rule that it is not a proper subject for a motion under Standing Order 43.

speechtext:
The Advisory Board established by the Disabled Persons Act has not met since 1959 and with the phasing out of the disabled persons program, it is not anticipated that there will be future meetings of the board. It consisted of two representatives of the government of Canada, appointed by the Governor in Council, and two representatives of each of the provinces with which agreements had been made, appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of each province. The federal representatives on the Advisory Board were the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the deputy minister of welfare. The minister in charge of welfare for each province, except Ontario, was one of the two provincial representatives. The other representative was either the deputy minister or the chief administrative officer in charge of

In the case of Ontario the representatives were the deputy minister of public welfare and either the director of welfare allowances or another senior administrative officer. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-32 now before us sets the whole question of the Canadian challenge for the present time as well as for the future. National interest must be based of course, on all Canadians being on the same footing. It must also be based on the same quality of life for everyone. But distributed as Canadians are in this great country of ours and administered by three levels of government, national interest in their case rests also and by far on the reconciliation of various social and economic interests at play in this country. Now, the identification of such social and economic interests depends on the full respect of the spirit as well as the letter of our Constitution, and of the jurisdiction of each Canadian province.
Therefore, it is right to say that Bill C-32 on oil and gas administration in this country sets the whole question of the Canadian challenge. Perhaps have I never before, at least in this House, had the opportunity to feel as responsible as a Canadian, as jointly liable in connection with the interests of my fellow citizens from the western provinces, who are very much concerned as we know about this bill and perhaps have I never felt as determined to understand and comprehend the concerns of fellow citizens in kin provinces. In the name of national interest, sections 36 and 52 of this bill come in direct contact with the prerogatives and vested rights of the so-called oil provinces.
I feel all the more I have to be alert on this Bill C-32 because once it is passed, all of us, whether from the

All Canadians, all Quebecers in particular, and the premier of the province of Quebec above all, must give very urgent consideration to the scope of this bill now before us. Today, there is talk about federal administration of oil and gas but if we are not careful today, tomorrow there may be talk about federal administration of power energy, or from another angle, territorial development and-
Mr. Speaker, in the very name of the Canadian challenge of modern times, in the very name of the type of Confederation in which we want to live Bill C-32 must provoke at the level of the people of this country, of provincial governments and information media, an information campaign on the stakes and the issues involved.
Mr. Speaker, consideration of Bill C-32 must actually bring people to their feet, have them talk with words of caution, warning and alertness.
Section 36 of the Bill reads as follows:
Where no agreement is entered into pursuant to section 22 with the government of a producer-province or any such agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, or, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the Governor in Council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which this Part applies that are produced, extracted or recovered in that province (hereinafter in this Division called the "exporting province").
Mr. Speaker, Canada or indeed the whole world must be experiencing a true energy crisis or about to experience such a crisis for the government to consider disregarding the vested interests of the provinces, for a central government to assume such powers.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, people will probably say: the facts are there, the world is undergoing serious energy problems; let us think, they will say, of the Arab-Israeli conflict, of the behaviour of oil-producing Arab countries on the world market, let us also remember above all that oil supplies in eastern Canada depend to a large extent upon imports, and therefore, is it not normal that we, as a government, should take appropriate action to meet the following objectives as stated in clause 21 of the bill:
(a)	to achieve a uniform price, exclusive of transportation costs, for
crude oil used in Canada outside its province of production;
(b)	to achieve a balance in Canada between the interests of consumers and producers in Canada: and
(c)	to protect consumers in Canada from instability of prices for
petroleum in the international markets.
With regard to those national objectives, may I just mention very briefly two specific points.
First, concerning the protection of consumers in Canada from instability of prices for petroleum in the international markets, I should like everyone here to remember how decisively our party fought in December 1973 to ensure equity and justice for the consumers of eastern Canada.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was waging this fight. On December 10, 1973, he said:
-this policy will result in a difficult and trying period for many individuals this winter, a promise of continued discrimination for
Oil and Petroleum
many years, a proof of increasing inequalities, and a guarantee of economic problems for eastern Canada.
In the name of justice, we, of the official opposition, demanded then and still demand that Canadian consumers be protected from the instability of prices in the international markets.
Secondly, and still from the point of view of the national objectives mentioned earlier, we must realize that we must also protect the interests of producers on behalf of the long term interests and needs of all Canadians.
On October 4 last, Mr. R. G. Reid, president of Imperial Oil Limited, said to the Ontario Institute of Chartered Accountants, and I quote:
The key to the development of future energy resources is the investor's confidence based upon risk-oriented public policies.

It is therefore crucial, Mr. Speaker, for this parliament and the government to keep in mind that the present energy resources available to this country exist because in the past the exploration and production of energy for domestic and export use has been a highly profitable endeavour.
When one briefly scans Canadian commercial history and views the extent to which a serious imbalance has existed between western and central Canada, particularly in terms of transportation and freight rates, one need not be particularly pro-western in one's approach to understand that the commercial unity of this country would be strengthened by rectification of this imbalance. One cannot help getting the impression that the present government's view of the degree to which profits from the oil industry can serve to rectify this imbalance is less than favourable.
I have to say, as a member of this House from a province that has itself in the past developed various profitable energy sources, that this type of view by the federal government is particularly short-ranged and somewhat narrow-minded. I can tell the House that when Hydro-Quebec moves to sell power to markets outside our province and outside our country, it is always done with a very real concern for ensuring the people of Quebec maximum profit for what is, after all, a renewable resource. Surely, therefore, we can understand the concern of jurisdictions wherein the major energy resource is non-renewable as is the case with petroleum products that there be similar, if not greater, protection in terms of increased profit yield for them, to ensure their economic vitality.
I believe we can find the way to protect the public interest, while ensuring that the exploration and processing of energy products, specifically in western Canada, remain activities not only profitable to private enterprise but profitable to provincial governments that are seeking to strengthen their own secondary industry and economic infrastructure through the yield that can be gained from the petroleum industry situated within their jurisdictions.
There is anxiety in the west that has caused many petroleum operations actively to consider moving their drilling rigs from Canada to other countries. Such a course of action, specifically in areas such as southern Alberta,

Oil and Petroleum
cannot be anything but a source of concern for anyone vitally interested in the health of the western economy. I believe parliament would do well to ensure that legislation presented to protect the public interest in the matter of petroleum and energy embraces a concept of public interest that has room for the type of fair profit within the oil industry that can, and will, play a significant role in prolonging the commitment of capital and other resources in the battle to find and to develop more natural resources for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the national objectives mentioned in clause 21, the national balance that is sought, all this must be worked out simultaneously by the central government and of each of the provincial governments. We federal and provincial parliamentarians must therefore reconcile the national and the regional interests. And, as I said earlier, one can see how this bill raises the whole question of the Canadian challenge and affects, if I may use this expression, the Canadian pattern itself.
Clause 36 as well as its counterpart clause 52 make it too obvious that in case of a disagreement, the federal government is automatically right. This does not take into account the reasons for which, in a particular situation, an oil producing province may not accept some proposal of the federal government. Yet, this directly concerns provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, on December 10 of last year, I said that this government was powerless to attack in depth the major problems and unable, in its search for adequate solutions, to reconcile the national and the regional interests. This government, under the pretext of acting for the common good, keeps infringing upon the principle of Canadian federalism itself.
The present federal government, probably the most centralizing one in all our country's history is certainly the government who has provoked and is still provoking, sometimes, almost on purpose the highest number of confrontations with the provincial governments.
Instead of trying to be, as the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) rightfully wishes-it is true, Mr. Speaker, that this was said during the last election campaign-instead of trying to be, and I quote: the life and soul of a common, collegial and global strategy the present central government is appointing itself, slowly but surely and month after month, the gravedigger of our Constitution.
Mr. Speaker, this government and this prime minister will be known to history as those under whom our Confederation will have been in danger as never before. We know, especially after the cry of alarm of last June 15 uttered by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) we know how threatening for the Confederation this alienation of the West is becoming. Transportation, the difficulties of the secondary industry and natural resources sector, those are problem areas where Western Canadians feel neglected by this federal government.
Should we now be surprised that the oil producing provinces, before approving, if ever, Bill C-32 demand, just

by so proof positive of Ottawa's good faith concerning the planning of industrialization policy, agricultural consolidation and restructuring of the railway freight rates in the Prairies.

I hope all parts of the country benefit from confederation. Nobody is disputing the value of the west to Ontario. It was certainly one of the arguments made to Ontario in order to get a national oil policy. The point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is that subsidies and assistance did not start with Alberta giving oil to the rest of Canada at a lower price. There is a long history of this kind of assistance, and Ontario did its part in helping the west to develop: it provided the market for western goods. Now the shoe is on the other foot. Ontario does not possess fossil fuel reserves. During the winter, we were in danger
November 4, 1974

of not getting any from offshore and it is a great comfort to Ontario to know there are resources in Alberta and we are not dependent upon the political whims of people outside the country to determine whether we freeze in the dark.
I have been very pleased by the speeches of western members on this subject. It seems that they understand the problem. Although they may not like accepting a lower price for crude oil than they could get on the open market, I think they understand that this has to be done in a confederation such as ours. I should, therefore, like to say "Thank you" to the people of the west. We in Ontario appreciate that we might not now have been in such good shape regarding energy had it not been for developments in Alberta.
We have gone a long way toward public intervention in the field of energy in order to assure supplies and to adjust the price. But we will have to go much further. Energy is so important, and the problem so complex, that I believe all energy supplies must come under public ownership-not just gas and oil but hydro and nuclear energy. And if the day comes that we are sufficiently intelligent to harness the tides or to obtain energy from the sun, this energy too would have to come under public ownership and be the heritage of the people of this country. We might even go beyond that and say it would have to be the heritage of the world: Canada might not be able to keep it to itself if the rest of the world needed it.
If we come to the conclusion that we are going to share our energy, surely our first responsibility is not to the richest country in the world, one that can find substitutes for cheap energy, but to the poorer nations. Those of us who complained about a continental oil policy did not do so because we did not want Canada to contribute in this sense. We objected because this resource was not going to the poor and the underdeveloped people of the world, but was going to those who are looking for cheap fuel and show no inclination of conserving energy by using their technology. I do not want to see any province or town in this country hoarding something and not feeling an obligation to anyone else, nor would I want this country to tell the rest of the world to look after itself.
We must move toward public ownership in order to solve the problem of conservation. One of the difficulties with free enterprise is that it must waste resources. The profits come from selling things to people whether they need them or not. Then there is a trade-off between the short-run interests of investors and the long-run interests as defined by the political process. I am not trying to make an ideological argument that public ownership is more holy than private ownership, Mr. Speaker. Some of us do favour public ownership over private ownership. However, the argument I am trying to make is essentially on the ground of public interest.
This is the kind of argument that was made when the Ontario government moved to take the hydro resources of the province under public ownership. In that case they were not socialist arguments, although people acted in a socialist and intelligent way by putting them forward. Their reasons were not ideological, but practical. The embryonic manufacturing industry of Ontario was in danger of falling under the control of outsiders who would also
Oil and Petroleum
need control of hydro power to further their interests. Almost everyone in Ontario felt that if the province were to develop, it would have to own its electrical resources. History has proven them wise. Ontario probably could not have developed in the way it has without public ownership of its energy, and today it is in the forefront in the development of energy, nuclear and electrical, and has some of the cheapest energy rates in the world. It was a fortunate decision that electricity was taken under public ownership in Ontario, and these arguments are as relevant today as they were in Adam Beck's time.
In putting forward these arguments I am somewhat encouraged by the receptivity of this government. The minister has found himself in difficult circumstances at times, but he has done a good job.

speechtext:
He had to learn fast, and he did. We found ourselves in an energy crisis last year, without an energy policy. Of course, we do not have much of an energy policy now, but we had nothing at all when the crisis hit. We can laugh now about the Minister of Supply and Services paying an outrageous sum for heating oil, but we would have cried had we run short of it. We would have said he should have bought it no matter what the price. It is regrettable, perhaps, that his business judgment was not sounder, but the important thing is that we came through an international energy crisis almost unscathed. It was done because of government intervention: the government was prepared to move in. It was done without legislation: there was no legislative authority for what the government did. This is an indication of the authority of government in our society. If a government is determined to act, it can say it expects the private sector to behave in a certain way because it is going to introduce legislation to make it so. It is quite clear. The private sector has no choice but to respond.
This situation is very instructive because the private sector concerned was almost entirely foreign-owned. We were afraid foreign ownership would make it impossible for people in this country to respond in an emergency. The message came through loud and clear. If governments in our society choose to exercise the authority given to them by the people of this country, they have infinitely more power than any foreign-owned corporation or privately-held organization. We have seen foreign corporations virtually run this country. That was not because intrinsically they had the power to behave in that way, but because our government refused to intervene. Because of the abstention of the government, these foreign corporations were able to make their will felt.
I know I speak for my colleagues when I say we were pleased that the government was prepared to intervene. One reason the government acted was the particular electoral arrangement at that time: I am talking about a minority government. For a long time there was a great spirit of co-operation between our group and the government, in terms of energy policy. People might say that at this point the government has a majority and no longer has to listen to the NDP. It probably does not. However, I

November 4, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
am confident that that kind of co-operation and response by the government to a national emergency made an impact on the government and the people in the Liberal Party. I notice with a degree of pleasure that even though Canada does not have a minority government now and we are not in a position to twist arms, some of the arguments we put forward last year have been put into effect. The government saw they were necessary. I am optimistic that we will continue to have a forward-looking policy and willingness by the government to deal with new problems as they arise.
I was interested in watching members on the government benches when my former leader spoke, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). Tremendous attention was paid to what he said. On many occasions the applause from the opposite side was a genuine expression of agreement with what he was saying. Therefore, I think that arguments once started, or paths once cleared, tend to have a way of being continued. The government was very reluctant to intervene in the situation to which I have referred. They have always been reluctant to do that. However, they now understand that it was absolutely necessary. The people of this country heartily approved of that kind of intervention, and I hope it will continue. I hope the government will listen to these arguments regarding public ownership, not in a narrow, ideological framework but as something that is necessary and useful for the development of future policy for this country.
At the present time, Interprovincial Pipe Line is dragging its feet in building the line to Montreal. They say they need guarantees. They do not know what the throughput, cost or price will be, and therefore are not prepared to do anything without guarantees. If it is necessary to guarantee rates, returns and everything else, why do we need Interprovincial Pipe Line? We might as well build the pipeline ourselves. We will probably be asked to guarantee their bonds. In fact, we did guarantee the bonds and the company operated with government guarantees. Why not build this section of the line under public ownership? I do not think a pipeline is the greatest thing to own publicly, but when you get to the point where you have to make all these concessions, you do not know how accurate company's figures are and you must ensure that the figures are not inadvertently exaggerated, you might as well go ahead and build the pipeline yourself.
It is well within the capacity of the Canadian government's resources-that is, the capacity of the Canadian public-to build this pipeline instead of delaying it. Let us not be lulled into a false sense of security. The tension seems to be off and the Middle East seems to have settled down. But it will boil up again. Are we to be subjected to this kind of pressure without being ready for it? I know we accommodated ourselves last time, but we should be much better off now than we were then. Last time we had to operate on an ad hoc basis because the government had not planned; it did not listen to the various proposals this party had put forward for years with regard to a pipeline to Montreal. We should proceed immediately to build a pipeline under public ownership, instead of trying to figure out what kind of subsidy or conditions the company wants. If we must go to a great deal of trouble, there does

not seem to be much point in having private enterprise build the pipeline.
We had considerable argument in committee about the Telesat Corporation. At the time the corporation was proposed, it was a troika arrangement: the idea was that the communications industry would own one-third, the government one-third, and one-third would be sold to the public. We put forward the same arguments. We said the rates would be regulated and the corporation could not lose money. If it appeared they were going to lose money, the government would adjust the rates. Why bring in the private investor or the telecommunications people into what was essentially a government idea? What is the point, when you are going to guarantee the corporation a return? Despite Telesat saying it was waiting until it got going a little before bringing in the private investor, it has not done so because they do not need the private investor. The private investor would be a hindrance to the corporation. Even though speeches are made about Telesat and lip service is paid to the proposition that at some point shares will be put on the market, those shares will never go on the market because it is not necessary. Telesat is an enormously successful corporation. They have made very good arrangements for the leasing of their communications channels and the public investor is not required.
The Canada Development Corporation is another example. We in this party argued for such a corporation. We saw the Canada Development Corporation as an instrument of national development, not as a way of offering the five-buck investor an extra place to invest his five bucks. We have a wonderful instruments for private investment. There are Canada Savings Bonds. Why do we need to create equity ownership in something as important as the Canada Development Corporation when the country needs a development corporation? The investors are satisfied with Canada Savings Bonds. The Canada Development Corporation is doing rather well. We are not happy that it is taking over profitable government corporations and then threatening to take them out of public control and put them into private hands by opening up their investment portfolios, but to this point they have managed very well without the private investor. In fact, they have probably done much better without him.
While the CDC says it is waiting until its portfolio fattens a little before putting its shares on the market, I suspect the same thing will happen as happened with Telesat. Private shares will never be issued simply because the CDC does not need the five-buck investor. Not only that, he would get in the way. There are already problems in the Canada Development Corporation, one of which is shameful for a public corporation. It took over Connaught Laboratories, which manufacture insulin. Because its sole term of reference is to make money, the corporation is still looking toward the day when it will put out investment certificates or provide an opportunity for the private investor. It is taking something which is essential and which should have been produced at cost, and trying to make a buck out of it.
Surely they can provide insulin at cost? They are making enough money from other investments to enable them to absorb the cost of manufacturing insulin. It was
November 4, 1974

important that CDC take over Connaught Laboratories because they had nowhere else to go. But it is also important that they recognize the social usefulness of providing insulin without making a profit on it. As long as that element is there, they must think in terms of the future- how things will look on the stock market. That is the problem. Where you do important work involving the future or public morality, to think in terms of profit is not same.
Profit has a useful purpose in unimportant things. If somebody wants to make a profit on shoes, good luck to them. You don't have to buy shoes to that extent. You can buy one kind, you can buy another kind; you can buy a cheaper one, or you can buy a more expensive one. You do not need to have the shoe industry under public ownership. There is no need for extensive regulation in such areas. But when it comes to programs such as medical care-which of course is almost entirely a public responsibility, as it should be-you recognize it, and now we have to recognize that a resource as vital as energy cannot be left to the shenanigans of the profit motive.
As to people in the field, I grant they have the best intentions in the world. I have met many people in the gas and oil industry and they seem like decent fellows I am not quarrelling with them for trying to act against the public interest because, I am sure many of them think their buccaneering is very much in the public interest and that the public benefits enormously from their buying and selling, and drilling, getting out and getting in, and all the rest of it. The point is, they are not in a position to act for the public, given the kind of attitude that they have and the nature of their industry, even if they wanted to.
What is the point of competition in energy? I know it is very convenient to have electricity going down your street, to have gas going down your street, to have oil being delivered to your house. It is very convenient to have all these modes of energy. But that is for a society that does not think there will be any shortage of energy tomorrow. To waste all that capital, to waste all those resources, to duplicate facilities-that is yesterday's society with its philosophy of sell, sell. Hydro advertises that it will give you a better deal than gas. That is competition. This brings me to the point I am trying to make.
Competition, by its very nature, by its very huckstering, is bound to be wasteful. We cannot afford to waste energy. The most compelling argument in favour of public ownership of energy is that it will eliminate duplication and waste. For the first time we would be able to plan energy. Let me cite one example of what happens when you do not plan. We think of bringing a gas line down from the Arctic. So what is the argument? The argument is that we will have to build so large a line that we will not be able to use all the gas that comes through it; therefore, let us take the three-quarters surplus in that line and export it until we can absorb its entire output.

speechtext:
Read the minutes and you will see that the government of Alberta put pressure on the federal government not to tax. The point is, these resource industries were let off the hook. The recommendations of the Carter commission were never enacted in that area. Had we been able to devise an intelligent tax system under which those industries were taxed on the same basis as manufacturing industries, we might have avoided much of the confrontation that now exists among the industry, the federal government and the provincial governments. But we failed miserably to achieve our goals through taxation. While those goals can sometimes be achieved through taxation, this is not a great example of taxation success.
The problem of scrutinizing and verifying the arguments made on both sides of the taxation question is so great that it is really pointless. You can argue that we can regulate. After all, why place oil and gas under public ownership? Why don't we do what we do with Bell Canada and regulate these industries? It works to some extent with Bell Canada. By and large, I do not know that the public would benefit substantially from public ownership of Bell Canada. As I say, I don't know and that is really the problem.
You get to the stage, when you regulate an industry, at which the cost of scrutinizing the industry, the cost of policing it, and its cost in terms of making that policing more difficult-like the CPR with its regressive analyses-becomes so great that at some point you throw your hands up and say, "We're just playing games with each other instead of getting on with the job, and it might as well come under public ownership." It is this sort of cops and robbers game, going back and forth with each other, that eventually leads to the need for public ownership. Regulation of Bell Canada is difficult enough, but imagine how much tougher it would be to regulate the oil and gas industry and to ascertain future plans.
The oil and gas industry has given us misleading information from Day One. When it suited its purposes to export, the industry gave us glowing figures of our oil and gas reserves. According to them, we have enough to last us practically for the next two million years. Then when they wanted a higher price, all of a sudden the story was different; we were told there was little oil and gas left and the industry required more money to go into new fields, otherwise in 15 or 20 years we would be short. It is inconceivable that something as important as energy is left to this kind of game playing.
We will have to spend $50 billion over the next ten years, perhaps more, to develop new forms of energy. Where do we start? If we start with the James Bay project, the tar sands project, building pipelines, developing nuclear energy, we shall need tremendous sums of money. We must approach the matter in a rational and intelligent way by allocating the resources at our disposal in the most effective manner. This means that we cannot finance our energy needs from the market system but must do so

through public saving and public investment. To do it in any other way would be an absolute waste.
I can give the House a great example of waste which, fortunately, turned out to be not so wasteful. This sometimes happens when you talk about waste, so I must be rather careful. In this instance, the result was more by accident than design. A lot of investment went into Alberta at a time when there was no need for it and no markets for oil. We operated our wells at something like 35 per cent capacity, tying up billions of dollars in equipment which had to yield a higher return. I see you are signalling, Mr. Speaker, so let me conclude by saying that I have advanced but a few of the many good arguments for our stopping this chaotic approach to private investment in the energy field and moving to a system of conservation and public works.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in this debate because, as several previous speakers have indicated, the topic under study is one of the most important facing the national as well as the international communities. One need only listen to the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), who speaks of it in a nationalistic vein, to become aware of it. Some of the members opposite covered every aspect of the energy problem to prive its importance.
To begin with, I should like to criticize the comments of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) who said-indeed that was his main argument-of all the opposition members from Alberta that his only objection to the bill is the fact that it gives rise to a confrontation between the rights of the provinces and those of the federal government. He indicated that the government members should protect the provincial rights. In fact, Mr. Speaker, we are federal members of parliament.
As far as the rights of the province of Quebec are concerned, I point out that they are directly protected by the provisions of this bill. Of course, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe has not seen anything, since the province of Quebec is paying $6.50 a barrel for its oil, the international price being $11.65. They save thus $5.15 a barrel on the oil imported in Montreal, because of the measures we are trying to implement and to apply efficiently, and which are contained in the bill under study.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is not at all a matter of taking powers from any province. The federal government has a national responsibility and he sees to carry it out with this bill, namely to ensure that the needs of the consumers in eastern Canada are met with western oil.
Mr. Speaker, since the federal-provincial agreement was entered into on March 31, we have in Canada a standard price for oil from coast to coast, taking into account the transportation costs. It is obvious that the province is the first to benefit from it. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec would have to pay $11.65 a barrel, while Ontario could have indulged in the luxury of paying less than $6 a barrel. The government has chosen to take its role seriously in spite of the position taken by the member for Saint-Hyacinthe, who asserts the rights of the province of Quebec and the other provinces. If we listened to him
November 4, 1974

and to his colleagues, we would give up our own responsibilities.

Yes, we studied the bill before the budget. I should like to take exception to what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said on second reading of the bill, then called Bill C-18. He said: "We will delay the passage of this legislation. We will study it with a fine toothed comb, and when we get it before the committee we will call witnesses galore and try and delay it as best we can". That is exactly what they did. The reason they did that is the same reason they are presently advancing, and the one the attorney general of Alberta gave when he appeared as a witness before the committee, namely, that it is a direct attack on provincial rights.
When Mr. Leitch appeared before the committee, he evidently had not bothered to read the bill beforehand, because if he had read it he would have seen that he was incorrect in his interpretation of its provisions. I suggest that no one has attacked the agreement which was reached on March 31; even the most recalcitrant members from Alberta have agreed it is essential for the stability of Canada's industrial complex and our economy as a whole. It is essential that there be some sort of equality regarding the cost of energy in this country; there is no doubt about that.
I should like to read what Mr. Leitch said when he appeared before the committee, as recorded at page 7 of committee report No. 15 of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. I am sure hon. members have read what he said. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) indicated that the principle of this bill had been negated by the agreement of March 31, and he repeated exactly what Mr. Leitch had to say. Mr. Leitch said;
Mr. Chairman, I wish to conclude by commenting on part III, the part to which our most fundamental objections are directed.
The hon. member for Calgary North is evidently in error. Throughout his speech he referred to part III as being under attack, but according to Bill C-32 it is part II. So he was referring to part III of Bill C-18.
Far from embodying a term of the first ministers' agreement it stands as a direct negation of the principles upon which that agreement was based.
It permits the executive council to terminate an existing agreement between a producer province and the federal government or to decline to negotiate a renewal agreement and to impose by unilateral action maximum prices on a natural resource owned by a province.
That is absolute balderdash. That is not what the section says at all. If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I will read what the section does say, because it has been referred to. It provides:
Where an agreement is entered into with a producer province under section 22, the governor in council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which
Oil and. Petroleum
this part applies that are produced, extracted or recovered in that province.
It speaks of an agreement reached under section 22. It provides for the entering into of agreements, and it also provides power to act if an agreement is not entered into or if it is unilaterally reneged by one of the producing provinces: it provides the federal government with the power to impose a price. Would any member of this House argue that the federal government does not have power over interprovincial or, indeed, international trade?
Would anyone argue that any individual province in this federation has power to impose negative prices, or has power to impose a higher price or a two-price system in respect of a commodity which it exports? Is there anyone who would say that as far as interprovincial trade is concerned, the federal government does not have the obligation to ensure that everyone, in every part of this country, has a fair shake and fair access to a commodity produced within this nation? Anyone who would deny that assertion would be attacking the very principles of this confederation.
We are all Canadians. No one can tell me that in northern Ontario the consumer does not have the right to receive natural gas because the province of Alberta, through Pan-Alberta, does not want to send its gas to northern Ontario. If Pan-Alberta has the right to do that, then it goes directly against the principles of confederation and the unity of this great country.
That is exactly the position that is being taken by members of the opposition. They are suggesting that they are doing this at great and tremendous sacrifice on the part of Alberta and Saskatchewan because they are subsidizing the rest of this country. I have some figures here of considerable interest which I should like to draw to the attention of the House. In 1972, before we started to have difficulty and at a time when royalties in the province of Alberta were 16 per cent of the price of oil at the well head, the total revenue for Saskatchewan and Alberta was $270,900,000, or roughly 44 cents per barrel. In 1973, when an export charge was levied and there was some federal interference-I will agree with that-the rate went up from 16 per cent to 22 per cent. Premier Lougheed said that was as far as he would go in respect of royalties, and the amount went up to $480,600,000.
In 1974, when this difficulty really occurred and the federal government interfered with the rights of the province of Alberta, the amount to those poor Albertans went up to $1,500 million. That does not include the export charge payable by the federal government of an extra $200 million. I just do not understand how they can say they are subsidizing the rest of the country when we are talking in terms of royalties amounting to $l3/i billion. Let hon. members on the other side get up and say those figures are wrong.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a special committee of inquiry on Crown corporations exercising financial, commercial or industrial activities be established to study the various Acts establishing such Crown corporations, the Crown Corporations Act, sections 76 to 88 of the Financial Administration Act, and all other laws concerning Crown corporations and to recommend to the House the adoption of a law regarding federal public enterprises; the committee should also study the following subjects without restriction (a) the legal rules pertaining to the employees of such corporations (b) their financial structure (c) the way in which they are financed (d) government control over said corporations (e) fiscal regulations (municipal, school, provincial and federal taxes (/) the status of the administrators (g) the privileges of such corporations resulting from their being "commis-

sioned by Her Majesty" (h) the status of the subsidiaries of these enterprises (i) their purchasing policy (j) the problem of auditing by the Auditor General of Canada or by private auditors (k) the appropriateness of State intervention in the economic field in the form of enterprises; and all other matters concerned. (By unanimous consent was allowed to stand and retain its position).
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to introduce this motion. I want to apologize first for my voice which mingled with that of demonstrators during the weekend. This does not mean that we must approve them, but we have to put up with them anyway.
I attach a great deal of importance to the motion on Crown corporations which I am introducing today. I am doing so for the third time. Each time, we manage to convince more and more members to support it.
What is the purpose of that motion? It is not to oppose the creation of Crown corporations nor to gloss over the activities of those corporations, but rather to throw some light on this whole governmental business.
To be more specific, Mr. Speaker, and to show the importance of that motion, I may say that it is a well known fact that the federal government now owns and operates an extensive industrial, commercial and even financial sector. For example, the government develops uranium mines through its Crown corporation Eldorado Nuclear Limited, and coal mines through the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The State is also engaged in mining prospection through the Quebec Mining Exploration Company, and oil exploration through Panarctic Oils Ltd. The State operates one of the largest railway systems in the world through the Canadian National Railways. It also operates a number of road transportation companies through the Canadian National Transportation Ltd., and the largest hotels in Canada through the Canadian National Hotel Ltd. The State is also involved in air transportation through Air Canada and Eldorado Aviation Ltd., in overseas shipping through the Canadian National and the Societe de Transport du Nord Ltee. Moreover, the State is one of the biggest producers of rubber in the world through its Polymer Corporation Ltd. It owns and operates one of the most extensive radio and television broadcasting network in the world through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It produces and sells electricity through Quebec Hydro and Ontario Hydro. It lends money at interest through the Industrial Development Bank, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Farm Credit Corporation and various deposit and savings funds. Mr. Speaker, based on the estimated figures to be found in the annual reports of these corporations, the turnover of the State at the present time amounts to nearly $20 billion per year.
Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely important area of financial and business activity for the government. By moving this motion dealing with Crown corporations, I wish to call the attention of all members to three very specific facts. First of all, because Crown corporations were created by the federal government, we feel they should be accountable to Parliament, so that each one would operate strictly within its own area of activity. Now the only information we can get from those corporations as members of Parliament is some kind of a summary of their activities included in their annual report. In other

words, parliamentary control is practically non-existent. I will give some examples later.
Second, the government owns and operates at present in Canada a hundred or so industrial, business or financial public enterprises, with assets of well over $20 billion. This contemporary phenomenon of a trading State raises many problems, for example: what will be the status of the trading State? What is its legal status? Several members do not know. Moreover, is the trading State subject to public law or to private law and, in both cases, in what circumstances? Then again, Mr. Speaker, few members, even those who have been in the House for a very long time, could answer this question. Will it have a mixed status proceeding from both private and public laws? Indeed, is it the private or the public law which applies in the administration of those acts? Finally, what control does Parliament have on those Crown corporations? That is another important question, Mr. Speaker. Why can the Auditor General, who is a parliamentary official rather than a government official, not audit the accounts of all the Crown corporations, but only those of a few? And yet, he would be the ideal person to exercise this parliamentary control on behalf of the members.
Another question one must ask, Mr. Speaker, is this: the main sources of information for the members on those corporate activities are: the annual report, the questions put on the order paper and the motions for the production of papers. But in those three cases, there are some serious shortcomings. What do we do with the annual report that we get at our office? We glance through it, we examine it, we scrutinize it paragraph by paragraph, but it does not say any more than what is written in it. It is a summary on administration. Its figures are roughly lined up and fail to inform the reader or the member on the internal operation of the corporation involved or on the role it plays within the economy.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a suggestion which seems most reasonable to me: reports should be referred to the standing committees of the House for consideration and review.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. members should be allowed to call officials of Crown corporations as witnesses in order to question them about annual reports. Thus would be recognized the important part hon. members play in the parliamentary control of Crown corporations. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that Crown corporations administer over $20 billion a year, which is close to the federal government budget and that is why hon. members should have their say in that matter.
Some ministers will reply that all this is quite right but that it is still possible to ask a written question or, as is commmonly said, to put a question on the order paper.
In other words, the question on the order paper is the one the hon. member puts there. The questions may be technical but in all cases, and here I quote Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, 4th edition, citation 181, para. (3), page 153:
A Minister may decline to answer a question without stating the reason for his refusal, and it is irregular to comment upon such refusal.

Mr. Speaker, this means that according to the rules, a minister could be justified in refusing to answer a valid question when, normally, the hon. members should get the required information.

It happens fairly often that the official of the company or the minister refuse to answer. The main reasons that are invoked are as follows:
Internal administration problems-A public corporation does not have to answer questions dealing with matters of internal administration For instance, in a public enterprise, management has sole jurisdiction over matters pertaining to the "appointment of personnel". It does not disclose information coming from personnel files of officials or employees.
Here, I refer to a speech made in Paris in 1946 by Sir John Anderson, on the subject of public corporations. I quote:
-Similarly, "it is not customary to ask Crown corporations (public enterprises) for information on their employees or other matters of internal administration.
Here I refer to the Hansard of the House of Commons, for June 23, 1963, question No. 663:
It concerns the salaries, amongst other things, of employees and officials of Crown corporations. I quote: Employees' salaries-A public Corporation will not answer a question whereby it is requested to disclose the salary level of an employee or a group of employees ... salaries are considered as confidential matters.
All we need here is to refer to Hansard reports for October 23, 1963, November 4, 1963, October 30, 1967 and December 20, 1967 to find examples of this type of answer.
On the salary matter, the Minister of Justice said:
"It is to be noted here that in the Public Accounts, while the individual salary of any Civil Servant above a given bracket is indicated, the salaries of all the employees of a Crown Corporation are grouped under one single item. A question in the House put to the responsible minister is virtually the only way to be informed of the individual salary of a Civil Servant or official of a Crown Corporation, if the minister is willing to reveal it." Recently, the CBC stated through the responsible minister, "it is contrary to the Corporation's practice to disclose the salaries paid to an individual".
I now refer to Hansard of January 15, 1969. And I could quote many other references to illustrate this type of answer.
With respect to fees and honorariums paid to officials, it says:
Fees and honorariums-A public Corporation will also refuse to reveal the fees paid to an individual: "It is not common practice to ask the CBC to disclose the fees paid to any individual."
At this point, I am referring to Hansard of December 4, 1963 and December 18, 1963.
And in a similar case, the hon. Minister stated:
The CBC informs me that due to the competition it has to face, it does not usually disclose the fees paid to the individuals it happens to hire.
And here, I refer again to Hansard, Mr. Speaker, but I will spare you the reference.
Fourth, and I quote:

Internal studies.-It was also decided that "it was against practice ... to disclose the names of individuals assigned to studies". The corporation considers such studies as "private documents" for internal use.
And here, I refer to Hansard of February 26, 1969, on page 5969.
Remuneration of the executive director.-"It is the practice... not to disclose any information from personnel records of officials and employees and this practice is supported by the Sessional Committee on Railways and the Shipping.
I refer here to the deliberations of this committee on December 20, as reported on page 5665, and on March 10, 1969, as reported in Hansard, on page 6387.
-This answer was given by Air Canada, the Northern Transportation Company Limited, Eldorado Nuclear Limited, Cape Breton Development Corporation and Polymer. However, the C.N.R. the C.O.T.C., the C.B.C., and the C.M.H.C.... disclosed the remuneration of their executive presidents. Therefore, there is no uniform and well defined practice.
I would also say to my colleagues on both sides of this House that it is not a partisan motion. Its aim is on the one hand to demonstrate to hon. members that Crown Corporations have a very important commercial, financial and judicial part to play in our society and that these corporations are the continuation of government activity and, finally, that their budget is over $20 billion.
Mr. Speaker, when a member of Parliament gets in touch with the Canadian Transport Commission, Air Canada or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, there is every possibility that, considering the well established practice in the House, he will not get an answer and most of the time the minister, even if he would like to answer, will have done so in private rather than publicly.
It shows, Mr. Speaker, that parliamentary control over those government creatures that are the Crown corporations is almost inexistent. On the one hand, the annual report is general and incomplete and on the other hand, questions on the Order Paper involve no obligation for the minister to answer and finally, the member of Parliament really cannot on his own authority, meet the chairmen of those corporations to get the information he wants.
So, Mr. Speaker, when the time comes for the House to approve estimates or subsidies to be applied against the deficit of the Canadian National or Air Canada or any other Crown Corporation, under the out-dated system that we have, the member of Parliament has the right, the obligation to approve subsidies to offset a loss but cannot, under the rules, make a corporation explain its deficit. It only does so in answer to a formal request from the minister who, then, must be kind enough to convey the information to us.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not discuss the motion any longer, so that my colleagues from both sides of the House will have the opportunity of expressing their views.
I just wanted to point out that this is not a motion for or against the corporations. My only aim is to have a special committee appointed to study the whole operation of the Crown corporations and their relation with Parliament, so that one day Parliament may have direct control over them.
