Mr. D, M. Collenette (York East): Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to talk to the motion before us in the name of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). The hon. member also has on the order paper a very complex bill on this subject. I studied over the weekend and I must say that a number of the points it makes are very relevant and should be looked into further. It seems there are two basic issues involved here. The first concerns the principle of Crown corporations; the principle of state intervention in the economy through Crown corporations. The second deals with the accountability to parliament of these corporations.
I do not wish to take the time of the House debating the philosophy behind the setting up of Crown corporations, but I should like to talk about their accountability to parliament. Part VIII of the Financial Administration Act relates to Crown corporations and incorporates provisions dealing with the control and accountability of such corporations as well as certain financial aspects of their operations. The act defines a Crown corporation as "a corporation that is ultimately accountable through a minister to parliament for the conduct of its affairs". It establishes a threefold classification of Crown corporations and develops a systematic pattern of relationships between corporations, on the one hand, and parliament and ministers on the other.
A departmental corporation is defined as one that is a servant or agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada responsible for administrative, supervisory or regulatory services of a governmental nature. It is, in fact, an ordinary department of government which has been given corporate status. It is subject to the direction and control of a minister and must rely on parliament for annual appropriations to cover its financial requirements. An agency corporation is one that is an agency of Her Majesty in right of Canada, responsible for the management of trading or service operations on a quasi-commercial basis, or for the management of procurement, construction or disposal activities on behalf of the Crown. Like a department or a departmental corporation, it is subject to a considerable degree of ministerial control. Although no very sharp line of division can be drawn, a distinction can perhaps be made between a department as the servant of a minister and a corporation as his agent.
A proprietary corporation is one that is responsible for the management of lending or financial operations, or for the management of commercial and industrial operations involving the production of, or dealing in, goods and the supplying of services to the public. It is ordinarily expected to conduct its operations without appropriations. It usually has a considerable amount of managerial freedom, and such control as the minister or the governor in council exercise over it is comparable to that of a shareholder who holds all or a major part of the stock of a private company.
While the minister is not usually held responsible for the day to day acts of the servants of a proprietary corporation, as he is for the acts of the officers of his department, he is often given a statutory right to intervene to give advice or directions and to demand an accounting so

as to ensure that there is an adequate measure of public control and accountability. A further distinction is that, since the amendments to the Income Tax Act in 1952, a proprietary corporation is subject to income tax.
A general pattern or blueprint of the financial relationships of Crown corporations with parliament and the ministry is set out in the Financial Administration Act, but this is not a complete and exhaustive statement of those relationships. Some Crown corporations are not listed in the schedules and are not subject to the act. Some are subject to specified sections of the act, while others that are listed are subject to it only to the extent that it does not conflict with the special statutes under which they were created or under which they operate. Thus, the Canadian Wheat Board, the Bank of Canada and its subsidiary, the Industrial Development Bank, are not listed in the schedules because of their special functions; they are excluded from the application of the act and are governed by the acts incorporating them.
When a Crown corporation is to be created, the usual practice is for parliament to enact a statute, which authorizes the establishment of the body and defines the corporate powers and purposes, outlines the basis of its financing and sometimes sets limits on its borrowing powers, determines the size and type of the board and sets the basis for the selection of members, the period of their tenure of office, remuneration, qualifications and grounds for removal. Some statutes, however, such as the Department of Defence Production Act, the Atomic Energy Control Act, the Research Council Act and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act, contain provisions delegating the power to establish corporations to the governor in council, a minister or other specified authority under the provisions of the Canada Corporations Act. Perhaps it might be better that all these Crown corporations have their terms of reference clearly defined by parliament.
Canadian Crown corporations, following business practice, are usually managed by boards of directors. There is no uniform practice in dealing with the constitution of the boards, their size and method of selection, or with the tenure of office, remuneration and removal of directors. Provision for each corporation is made in light of its special needs and circumstances. I think the hon. member made a very good point. Perhaps the public does deserve to have closer scrutiny of the salaries paid to officials of Crown corporations and of their general hiring and management practices.
Appointments to the boards are usually made by the governor in council rather than by a minister, although a minister customarily makes the recommendations and in case of companies incorporated under the Canada Corporations Act he may actually make the appointments. It is not the practice to appoint ministers to the boards of Crown corporations. When departmental representation is required, civil servants are usually named, but the majority of the part-time members of boards are selected from outside the public service. The remuneration of board members is usually fixed by the governor in council. However, when a civil servant is named to a board, he serves without additional remuneration.
There has been some discussion by hon. members of members of this House sitting on the boards of Crown
November 4, 1974

corporations. I think this aspect of a member's parliamentary life should be looked into. As a freshman member of parliament, I think it would be very useful to participate in decisions affecting Crown corporations which are involved in so much of the economic life of Canada. Indeed, one of my colleagues, a little later, may delve into this aspect of members participating on boards.
Except for a modest provision for making working capital advances to Crown corporations, the Financial Administration Act contains no specific authority for financing the capital and operating requirements of the corporations. The methods of raising funds for the capital purposes of the corporation are usually set out in the company's statute of incorporation, but provision may also be made in special statutes, as in the case of the Canadian National Railways, or in votes in annual appropriation acts, as in the case of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the National Harbours Board.
In general, capital requirements may be financed from internally generated funds and other reserves of the corporation, in so far as these are available and are not required by law to be paid into the consolidated revenue fund; from the sale of bonds or debentures to the public with or without the guarantee of the government; from loans, advances or outright grants out of the consolidated revenue fund; from the sale of equity stock to the government; or from borrowings in the private sector secured by the pledging of corporate assets. Where a corporation's funds are not sufficient to finance its operating requirements, financial assistance for all or part of its programs is usually sought from the government. This is usually extended through outright parliamentary grants unless there is a reasonable expectation that operating deficits will be offset by surpluses within a relatively short time.
Certain corporations have the power to borrow from the public. The instances in which they have been able to borrow from the public without a government guarantee have been confined to short-term requirements, and usually from the chartered banks with which they normally transact business. Their long-term borrowings from sources other than the federal government have usually required a government guarantee. Where such a guarantee is involved, parliamentary authority is required; in addition, the terms and conditions of the loan itself, as well as the guarantee, require prior approval by the governor in council.
Government loans to Crown corporations for the financing of capital expenditure programs, whether such programs involve the acquisition or construction of assets, the lending of funds to the public or the strengthening of a corporation's working capital, are, in almost all instances, interest-bearing. The interest rates for loan drawdowns are usually set quarterly on the basis of the cost to the government of borrowing funds for a comparable period, plus approximately one-eighth of 1 per cent to cover other costs not reflected in the interest rate, and these rates are applicable for the whole period of the loan. Usually, loans are repayable over the period of the loan, with periodic payments of principal and interest.
Where loans are made for the acquisition of fixed or physical assets, the repayment schedules are usually based on the expected useful life of the assets for which loans
Crown Corporations
are incurred. In some instances the periods are stipulated in the applicable legislation. No attempt is made to deal with each individual asset and its expected life but, instead, with groups of similar assets. For example, in the case of a power plant, the amortization period is based on the expected useful life of the plant as a whole, rather than on its individual parts. Where loans to the corporation are for the purpose of relending to the public, the repayment period is usually based on the period or periods over which the corporation in turn receives repayment.
Controls operate in a number of ways, but the most significant are the provisions of the statute under which the corporation was created. These encompass the nature and constitution of the governing board and the appointment and removal of members or directors; the approval of budgets and proposed methods of financing; the determination of the criteria to be followed in ensuring that satisfactory accounting records are maintained and financial administration procedures followed; the requirements of an independent and effective audit; and the preparation and submission of adequate annual and other reports which fully disclose the activities, operations and affairs of the corporation.
It is here that I take exception to the remarks of my colleague from Lotbiniere, in that I believe the reports of Crown corporations do, in the main, serve their purpose. They inform the members of the House and the general public of areas in which they have been active during the year and reflect the general record of the corporation. There are other areas of control such as the approval of bylaws, contracts and the salaries of senior officers, the right to issue directives and the requiring of information. Not all of these are of equal importance or of uniform application to all corporations.
The basic financial control of the Crown corporation is through requiring the submission and approval of budgets. Under section 70 of the Financial Administration Act all agency and proprietary corporations prepare annual capital budgets which are submitted to the appropriate ministers, the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance, for their recommendation to the governor in council. After approval by the governor in council, the budgets are laid before parliament. Major projects or expenditures are set out in the budgets, including estimates of proposed capital expenditures for land, buildings, plant and equipment, increases in working capital, amounts required for redeeming maturing indebtedness and, in the case of those companies which administer lending programs, the amounts required for making loans.
An estimate is usually made of the over-all cost of a program, of the estimated commitments for future years, and of the cash required for the year under review. Some indication is also given of the source^ from which the funds required will be obtained. The approval of the budget does not constitute an authority for the corporation to borrow, nor does it signify an undertaking on the part of the government to lend or to guarantee loans. These powers must be specifically granted by parliament, either annually or in a general continuing authority, and the terms are usually subject to the approval of the governor in council.

November 4, 1974
Crown Corporations
Agency corporations are also required to submit their operating budgets for the approval of the two ministers, the appropriate minister and the President of the Treasury Board, but there is no specific requirement to lay these before parliament.
Proprietary corporations are not required to submit operating budgets, presumably on the ground that they should be freer than agency bodies in the management of their own affairs. Nevertheless, there are several exceptions. For example, the Canadian National Railways and, as the hon. member mentioned, the Cape Breton Development Corporation are required to submit both operating and capital budgets to parliament. However, the nature and magnitude of operations of both agency and proprietary corporations are subject to parliamentary approval when funds are sought to cover operating deficits.
Statutes of incorporation usually require a corporation to maintain an accounting system satisfactory to the responsible minister. Under the Financial Administration Act a corporation must keep proper account books and related records, and may make provision for reserves for the depreciation of assets, uncollectible accounts and other purposes, subject to the direction of the Treasury Board.
Annual statements of accounts are required, for which standards of disclosure and reporting comparable to those required of private companies are established. These are to be prepared in accordance with such directions as to form as the Treasury Board may give. In addition, a corporation must make such other reports of its financial affairs as the appropriate minister requires.
The auditor of a Crown corporation is usually designated in the statutes of incorporation, although some acts merely provide for an appointment to be made by the Governor in Council. When the designation is by statute the Auditor General is usually named, but when an act provides for appointment by the Governor in Council the choice in the past has been made from private auditing firms. However, even in the latter case the Auditor General is eligible for appointment; the Financial Administration Act provides that, notwithstanding any other act, he may be appointed the auditor or a joint auditor of a Crown corporation. I think this goes far enough to answer the point brought out by my colleague.
The Financial Administration Act gives comprehensive directions embracing both the accountancy and authority aspects of the audit. The auditor of each corporation must report annually to the appropriate minister, and the general form of his report is prescribed. Each Crown corporation must submit its annual report, together with its financial statements and the auditor's report, to the appropriate minister, who must lay its report before parliament within 15 days after he receives it, or, if parliament is not then in session, within 15 days after the commencement of the next session.
In 1951 the Public Accounts Committee recommended that the annual report of each Crown corporation should be referred for study to a select committee of the House, and that the annual reports of all Crown corporations should be published together in one section of the public accounts.

Usually some direction as to the disposition of surplus moneys of Crown corporations is given in the statutes of incorporation.
Agency corporations are usually required to surrender their profits to the Receiver General. The Canadian Commercial Corporation, which may retain for its own purposes all moneys received in the course of its business, is an exception, although the Minister of Supply and Services may direct it to pay over to the Receiver General any of the moneys administered by it that he considers to be in excess of requirements.
The proprietary corporations usually have a greater degree of freedom in using their own funds, and many are permitted to retain their profits. However, the practices followed differ from corporation to corporation. For example, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Farm Credit Corporation, and the Royal Canadian Mint may retain their earnings to establish reserve funds, but when the statutory limits on these have been reached all additional earnings are payable to the Receiver General.
The Northern Canada Power Commission may retain its surplus earnings, to be used, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, in the reduction of rates to consumers. The Export Development Corporation may pay excess moneys to the Receiver General on demand. The Financial Administration Act contains a variation of this provision, whereby the Minister of Finance and the appropriate minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may require a corporation to pay to the Receiver General any moneys considered to be in excess of requirements, such excess to be used to discharge any debt owing by the corporation to the Crown, or to be applied as revenues of Canada. This provision, however, is operative only when it is not inconsistent with any legislation applicable to a corporation.
The Minister of Finance exercises a general control over the designation of bankers and depositories for Crown corporations. Under the Financial Administration Act a corporation, with the approval of the minister, may maintain accounts in the Bank of Canada and in such banks in Canada or financial institutions outside Canada as he may approve. Normally commercial banking facilities are used, although in a few cases the Bank of Canada has been designated as the depository for a corporation's bank balances. There is a further provision in the act authorizing the Minister of Finance, with the concurrence of the appropriate minister, to direct a corporation to pay all or part of its money to the Receiver General, to be placed to its credit in a special account in the consolidated revenue fund.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INQUIRY TO STUDY ACTIVITIES OF AND LEGISLATION RESPECTING CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) is similar to the one I moved a few years ago, but, in fact, his goes further. Mine only suggested that there be at least one member of parliament on the board of directors of every Crown Corporation, to ensure a better control of the expenditures the government makes through its corporations. The hon. member for Lotbiniere thinks that it might be convenient to form a special committee of the House to study every aspect of Crown corporations. It is a good suggestion, although I do not necessarily agree with
November 4, 1974

everything the hon. member said. It seems to me that this question should have been discussed long ago.

When I say I do not agree with everything the hon. member for Lotbiniere has said, what I mean is I think he has decreased his chances of having this motion passed by the House. It is not that I disagree with anything specifically in his motion, as I think it is an excellent motion, but the fact that he says we must have a special committee look into the aspects of each and every Crown corporation-at least that is the way I interpret it-means that we would have a committee studying all of these Crown corporations for a very long time. I do not know how many there are, but I think there are over 40. Therefore, for the simple reason of practicality I could not go along completely with the motion of the hon. member.
If the hon. member were to propose his motion in a different way so the House could consider asking for the subject matter to be referred to the committee I think his motion would be more acceptable to the House, and I would encourage him to do so. This is a subject that has been very dear to my heart since I have been a member, and I have spoken about it over the years.
I feel very strongly that as members of parliament we come here to represent the people of Canada and yet are unable to represent them properly simply because we have no control over certain aspects of government spending. It is suggested that Crown corporations must be autonomous and independent. We can all realize why, under certain conditions, a Crown corporation must be autonomous, but there certainly must be some kind of control, some kind of answerability, whereby Crown corporations must exercise responsibility to the people of Canada through their elected members who speak on their behalf.
Many times in this House and in committee we have asked a minister for some information, or have made a suggestion concerning a Crown corporation under his aegis, and have been told that that body is autonomous, is independent, and therefore he will have to refer the matter to that corporation.
In many instances the minister seems to have absolutely no control over such bodies. We could take almost any Crown corporation as an example. The CNR is an obvious one. The CBC is another. No one wants to control the press of this country. I am sure no one would suggest that the government should control the CBC. On the one hand while no one suggests the government should have control over the press, on the other hand such a body as the CBC should not have licence-which very often is the term used in the name of freedom of the press-to do whatever it wishes. There must be certain norms established, and I say this must come through the voices of the representatives of the people.
I wonder whether perhaps the hon. member would consider making an appeal to the government on the basis that it really is not necessary to have Crown corporations examined in detail by a committee but rather that we should have an opportunity in committee to examine all the general aspects of Crown corporations, and particularly the answerability feature.
Crown Corporations
In the past I have suggested that members of parliament should be members of the boards of directors of Crown corporations. This has been done in some provinces. It has also been done in some other countries. However, this has not met with complete approval in this House up until now. Perhaps this is not the answer, but at least it is a suggestion. It would seem to me that a special committee, such as the committee proposed by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), could be the vehicle to examine the feasibility and the pros and cons in respect of members of parliament being on those boards. The committee could examine all the other aspects having to do with the answerability of these corporations to the people of Canada through their representatives. So I would make that suggestion to the hon. member. Perhaps he might see his way clear to do this.
I rather think the government would be of a mind to accept that kind of approach. From what I understand- and I hope this is the case-more and more items discussed here in private members' hour, whether by way of notices of motions or specific bills, will be referred to committees, or at least their subject matters will be so referred. This does not necessarily mean that the government says it will grab the ideas proposed, but rather that it will allow such items to go to a committee for study. I believe this is a great step forward because, in the last few years, it has developed that private members' hour has been nothing but a time for members to come forward with their favourite ideas only to find that no one would listen, and that motions and bills would simply be talked out. It certainly is not my desire to talk out this particular motion. I simply want to say I would encourage the hon. member to use this approach to the government, and I would encourage the spokesman for the government to recommend that this matter be referred to a committee so that the general aspect can be studied in detail.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INQUIRY TO STUDY ACTIVITIES OF AND LEGISLATION RESPECTING CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to discuss the subject of Crown corporations. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) is to be commended for his persistence. As he indicated at the commencement of his remarks I think he has more and more won approval from members of this House for the kind of action or stance he wishes to take.
The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) favours a somewhat different approach, namely, the appointment of members of parliament to boards of directors. When one realizes there are approximately 40 Crown corporations perhaps it is not appropriate to take this position. However, I do not think the hon. member for Cochrane would suggest that a member of parliament should sit on the board of directors of each Crown corporation. Most assuredly there are some corporations in respect of which I believe there would be some merit in considering his suggestion.
Having been a member of the Public Accounts Committee for some years, I am aware of the frustration experienced by members of that committee when it is felt that a particular Crown corporation warrants more thorough or in-depth investigation. I remember, I believe it was during the first parliament I was here, that of 1968-72, when we had an opportunity to study the expense
1030

November 4, 1974
Crown Corporations
accounts of CBC personnel travelling abroad, and also the expense accounts of CBC personnel travelling within Canada.
The Auditor General had conducted quite a thorough study at that time. He compared the hotel rates being paid in various places such as Winnipeg, Victoria and Quebec. I think it is worthy of comment that the Auditor General could not find fault with the personnel of the CBC. If anything they were found to have been quite frugal in the manner in which they used expense money, recognizing that after all it was the taxpayers' money.
The frustration we experienced was when the CBC management decided that something was to be filmed in Toronto and decided to move 14 or so personnel from Winnipeg to the Toronto area. All we could study was whether or not those 14 people had lived within the limits of their expense accounts in respect of hotel accommodation, taxi cabs, meals and so on. What we could not get at in that committee was the reason why it was necessary to have 14 people travel from Winnipeg to Toronto. We could not determine whether the personnel might have been available in Toronto, or whether it might have been possible to use some camera men, for instance, under contract. That was the type of frustration felt by the committee.
I think that is the type of problem the hon. member for Lotbiniere and the hon. member for Cochrane are trying to solve, that is, that when board decisions are made to move personnel or to move them by a particular means of conveyance, a committee should have an opportunity to determine why such a particular decision was taken. This, I believe, is an example of the frustration experienced by many members of parliament in respect of Crown corporations.
To my way of thinking-and the hon. member for Cochrane touched on this-the hon. member's motion is too broad to be accepted by the government. In other words, he is suggesting a special committee of inquiry seemingly to look into all Crown corporations. Yet he was quick to point out that he is not challenging Crown corporations, he is not saying that there is anything wrong with them but that there might be something wrong. What he is saying is that we do not have an opportunity to do an in-depth study of Crown corporations under the present circumstances.
I was impressed by the research work done by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette). I must say quite sincerely that listening to his address today I learned a fair amount about Crown corporations. Obviously when asked to participate in this debate he did so seriously, and did a tremendous amount of research. I must also say quite frankly that my interest in Crown corporations has been fairly parochial. I was interested in the workings and machinations of Polymer, now called the Polysar Corporation. But I think the hon. member indicated a broader interest. He also showed us the manner in which one can check out and study budgets if one is moved to take that particular course of action.
I do not know how closely the hon. member for Lotbiniere was listening to the address of the hon. member for York East, but I would commend it to him. There was a

tremendous amount of information contained in it which he could study. He might say, "If that is the way that certain Crown corporations operate, I really do not think I am too interested in them. There seem to be enough safeguards, and if I want to do so, I can find out by either going to the minister, by putting a question on the order paper, or by attending the committee."
Listening to the hon. member's comments I found that he was good enough to point out that there were areas where it might not be such a bad idea to have a more thorough investigation into a particular Crown corporation, in support of the stance of the hon. member for Cochrane.
So we seem to be of one mind here. The only differences are in the methods or means of approaching this, whether we establish a special committee of inquiry, whether there is sufficient protection now to protect the Canadian taxpayer, or whether we need members of parliament or other people appointed to represent the government on these boards of directors and to report directly to parliament. I think that is the thrust of the motion we have before us today.
I support the idea that all these motions should not be talked out. In the six years that I have been here I have heard some excellent ideas advanced during the private members' hour. I have participated in several of them to the point where the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) once referred to me as the hatchet man in the private members' hour. However, I was sincerely interested in the subject matter of the debate and wanted to participate in it.
Unfortunately when one is on this side-and most of the motions emanate on the other side, which is appropriate because we here have other avenues of promoting our ideas-one ends up speaking for five minutes only and being called a hatchet man, whereas the individual who introduced the motion might have taken twenty minutes. This makes it difficult for us to express our judgment. But there are instances of ideas put forward in private members' hour being adopted, and probably this is what encourages the hon. member for Lotbiniere to keep pressing the point he is making today.
Let me say, on a sad note, that when a Canadian destroyer had a fire and explosions on board, this came to my attention because one of the crew members on that ship was from my riding and he died in the course of the accident. Under the rules of the Department of National Defence, which were still a hangover from wartime, a sailor had to be buried on land closest to where he was killed, even though, as in this case, he had never set foot on it. Then there was the ridiculous situation of a man in the Canadian army who went on a course to Great Britain, and on the train from his port of landing died from a heart attack. He had to be buried in Great Britain although he had only just got off the boat which took him there.
The Americans, in spite of the great number of soldiers who were killed in the war in Viet Nam, established a policy whereby people killed on active service were brought back to their native land if their families so wished. I put forward a motion that the families of Canadian personnel killed in the course of performing their duty should have the option to have them buried in
November 4, 1974

the place where they performed their duty, or brought back home.
Frankly, I am not getting off the subject, Mr. Speaker, but rather stressing this point to indicate to the mover of the motion that there is hope that motions such as mine and the one before us might be adopted and accepted by the government. If a bill is introduced, possibly it will not be accepted but the subject matter of the bill might be proceeded with and studied by a committee.
I thought the hon. member might be interested in a few facts. In reference to Crown corporations let me point out that today there are approximately 40 of them. When I did my research on that subject I found it mind boggling. I did not realize there was that much necessity for government involvement. I think the point made by the hon. member is good, that we have to keep our eye on these Crown corporations.
Let us look at the short period of ten years from 1963 to 1973. Legislation was passed to create a number of Crown corporations. For example, in 1963 the Economic Council of Canada was created; in 1966, the Company of Young Canadians; in 1966 the National Arts Centre Corporation; in 1967 the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, again in the same year the Canadian Film Development Corporation, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, the National Museums of Canada; in 1969 the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. I will not go on with them. If I were trying to kill time I could list several others that are here, but I do not wish to do that.

What disturbs me, and I am sure disturbs hon. members, is that from time to time legislation must be introduced to increase the powers of existing corporations to enable them to fill the changing demands of the areas which they were set up to serve. I am sure that this is necessary, but I think it should be scrutinized very carefully because I do not like to see the government getting involved in it.
When I see a Crown corporation expanding, I ask myself: is that not a role that could be better played by private industry? My view is that if it can be, we have no business there. Let private industry look after that. There may be areas where we must move in, and the one which we have heard about most is the Cape Breton Development Corporation. I think it was set up in 1967 to carry out the rationalization of the coal industry, and to broaden the base of the Cape Breton economy by making it less dependent on coal. I think this is where the government had an obligation to move in to help the area.
