sCanada Pipe Lines. The solution is to require Tran-sCanada to act as a common carrier, Mr. Speaker. That would produce a multiplicity of buyers and suppliers. There would be a competitive market, and the price of natural gas would reach the proper level. Canadians would be spared the expense of a tremendous bureaucracy to implement this part of the bill, as well as the tensions of federal-provincial conflicts.
There are some fundamental questions that western industrial producers as well as the provinces would like to have answered, Mr. Speaker. Who would receive the additional revenues? Is the government going to invent some new kind of tax to skim off the cream? Why is it that the minister has not introduced general price controls on all energy? If there is in effect a national policy of price controls on energy, why are hydro, coal, wood, uranium and all sources of energy not included? Westerners might be forgiven for thinking that it might be because these other commodities have to be purchased from provinces other than Alberta.
Part IV of the bill deals with cost compensation, which is a tremendously complicated method of arriving at the subsidy level for oil imported by eastern producers. When asked in committee why there was such complexity, government spokesmen said they wanted to avoid paying some companies too much. So they came up with this complicated system which removed the incentive to shop around for the best price on the international market. That resulted in crude oil costing less in Montreal than in Toronto.
According to the national oil policy which came out in dribs and drabs over the past year there was to be a uniform price across Canada, based on the Montreal price less the cost of transportation. But now the Toronto price is higher than Montreal. That is a good thing for the people of Montreal, of course, but how is a pipeline justified in that case? I wonder if Interprovincial Pipe Line Company is having second thoughts? Why build a pipeline when the system in place gives Montreal a cheaper oil than would be the case if pipeline tariffs had to be paid?
Part V contains a provision that Bill C-18 contained, namely, that a federal civil servant can walk into the office of any premier in Canada and seize any files he chooses. That is an absurd provision, to say the least. It is another example of the arrogance of this government.
The saddest aspect of this whole energy federal-provincial confrontation of the past year and a half is what is happening to the country in terms of our future economic viability and loss of potential. Right now the oil and gas industry of Canada is, essentially, in neutral. It is fulfilling commitments made a year or two ago, but not undertaking any new commitments to explore and develop new reserves.
Statistics indicate about a 10 per cent drop in drilling activity. That in itself is alarming. We should be increasing our exploration and development in order that we will be self sufficient in the future. These statistics do not however show how bad the situation really is because the companies are in neutral.

A lot of the expert personnel who are necessary for healthy exploration and development activity are leaving Canada. I refer to the drilling companies and their personnel. So far we have lost 37 or 38 rigs. These are long footage rigs, the most expensive and most difficult to replace. Even worse, we have lost the personnel to go with these rigs. We have lost seismic crews, geochemists, geologists and geophysists. These are Canadians who were born and educated in this country. They did not want to move, but things have come to a halt. In order to maintain their livelihood they have moved to Denver, Dallas or Houston.
People in the inudstry have indicated that if we went back to the post March 27 mood that existed in the prebudget period when it looked like the energy situation was straightened out, it would take two years to restore the previous effort. We have lost two years, and every day of delay prolongs that.
In order to make any sense whatsoever, a national oil policy must have as its prime priority the development of sufficient supplies for Canada to remain self sufficient. We have the geological potential to be self sufficient in conventional supplies. We have the tar sands with their enormous potential, as well as enormous reserves of other forms of energy. It would be a tragedy, to put it mildly, if we did not develop this potential and did not remain self sufficient in the future. I might say there is a very good possibility we will not do so if things remain the way they have been, Mr. Speaker.
There is continual federal-provincial bickering and changing of rules. Commitments made one month are broken the next. All this has shattered the confidence of the industry. A severe decrease in activity has resulted. This country's long-term potential is being endangered. How do we get out of this situation?
It is essential that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the government start the ball rolling by making some gesture to indicate they have lost interest in maintaining this fight. The provinces would like to see it come to an end. They would like to see a mood of optimism and enthusiasm restored in the oil and gas industry. They would like to see these companies develop the reserves that Canada will need.
A good place to start would be by removing clause 36 of this bill which states the federal government can unilaterally impose its will on the producing provinces. Removal of that clause would demonstrate that the government has confidence in the goodwill and interest of Canadians in other parts of Canada in the future of this country, and is willing to gamble on co-operative federalism. If it made that simple gesture it would go a long way toward improving the atmosphere that exists, and putting an end to this ceaseless bickering.
I do not think it can be said often enough or loud enough that Canada is the only western industrialized nation that is self sufficient in energy. We have an opportunity that we have not had in the 107 years since confederation. We are in a good position vis-a-vis our competitors.
It is unforgivable that the government would be wasting its energy fighting and scrapping over who is going to get what chunk of the cream rather than concentrating on how we, as a nation, can take advantage of this opportu-
November 4, 1974

nity we have now. It is unforgivable that that should be the prime motivation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). Instead of scrapping about the revenue, and worrying about how much will go to the producing provinces and how much to the consuming provinces, they should work this out. They are good people, those who are involved in the other governments of Canada. They are just as fine Canadians as those who come from Toronto Rosedale.
The opportunity that now exists will not exist in perpetuity. There is a limited time frame in which we must seize this opportunity. Any sensible Canadian who thinks about it will agree that the time is ripe now to stop bickering and get on with the building of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when introducing Bill C-32, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) concluded by stating:
The objectives which it seeks to achieve are for the most part familiar to members as being now well-established components of an integrated national energy policy.
I challenge that statement. I believe this government in no way has shown an integrated national energy poiicy for this country.
We in the province of Ontario are particularly concerned about the government's handling of this entire question. In Ontario we need essentially two things. In energy we need security of supply. Secondly, we need a pricing of our energy that leaves us competitive, internationally, and with consumers of petroleum products in the other provinces of Canada.
In many ways the government has not suitably protected Ontario with regard to those two matters. For example, the bill we are debating this evening deals with transferring funds raised by the federal government through an export tax so that they may be used to compensate importers on the eastern side of the country. Surely we have to ask ourselves why.
Why is it necessary, in a country such as Canada which produces enough domestic oil to serve the entire nation, that we have to go through a complicated taxing and compensation plan in order to have a one oil price in the nation? It comes down to one very simple fact. While we have the domestic reserves in Canada we do not have the domestic transportation system to deliver those reserves throughout the nation. I say this because I believe the government could have put a suitable transportation system into place and averted the problem of having to deal both domestically and internationally with such a vital matter as the distribution of our available oil.
A year ago I remember being in the lobby watching television when our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came on and said in a firm voice that a pipeline between Sarnia and Montreal would be built. Yet there is still hesitation on the part of the government. As I say, it is time the government treated the building of a pipeline not only to Montreal but to the east as a national priority, and got on with the job.
It has been suggested by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that the pipeline should be paid for by
Oil and Petroleum
means of charges on the tariff to be borne by consumers in Ontario. I challenge this concept. What the minister is suggesting, in effect, is that the $180 million the pipeline will cost should fall on those who use it in the province of Ontario and that, in the event not one drop should go east, the entire cost would be a charge on the consumers of Ontario. We believe this is unreasonable and that the government should either work out a suitable arrangement with the interprovincial pipeline people for the building of the line, including government guarantees if necessary, or, failing that, build the pipeline itself. In this way security of supply would at least be accorded to the extent that reserves are available in Canada.
Let me touch on the minister's speech in another regard. In introducing the bill he mentioned that there is one oil price throughout Canada. I challenge this. The fact is- though I notice the hon. gentleman very cleverly glossed it over-there is not one oil price across the nation. For example in Montreal today oil costs 70 cents less than it does in Toronto. That is about 2 cents a gallon when translated into the refined product. Here again we are dealing with an aspect I find rather alarming.
The minister claims there is one price. But he does not make it clear that since transportation costs are approximately 70 cents, the price of the product in Montreal is about $6.50, and in some cases as low as $6.00, leaving a minimum differential between Toronto and Montreal of 70 cents per barrel. Translated into gross terms this means Ontario is paying more than $200 million a year more for oil than consumers in Quebec.
A pipeline must be built, and the pipeline must be reversible. A time may come when foreign crude is cheaper than oil we can produce domestically, or we may find that eastern resources will be available to people in Ontario. In either case we believe it important that a pipeline be built without delay so that Ontario may be placed in a more advantageous position.
When he appeared before the committee which was dealing with this measure, then known as Bill C-18, the minister made it clear that the price of oil in Montreal was to be $7.20. As reported at page 12:25 of the minutes of the Standing Committee on Natural Resources and Public Works, issue No. 12, for Wednesday, April 24, 1974, Dr. Ian Stewart said the base price in Montreal would rise to $7.20. I believe that when this question is dealt with in the committee the minister should be prepared to explain why the figure has risen since April of this year as contrary to the minister's declared intention with respect to the one price policy he announced last April.
Another fundamental question dealt with in this bill is that of raising revenue through an export tax on one sector of the industry and using it, at least in part, to compensate importers of oil. I believe that in committee the minister should be prepared to explain what safeguards are intended to ensure that there will not be an international rip-off here. We must bear in mind that in many cases the multi-national corporations which, on the one hand, are exporting our oil, are, on the other, involved in the importation of oil to eastern Canada.
Again in committee last April, it was revealed by one of the officials in the minister's department that approximately 90 per cent of the oil involved in Canadian imports

November 4, 1974
Oil and Petroleum.
is oil imported into Canada by multi-national corporations which, in turn, are engaged in the production of oil in western Canada. Surely when we are dealing with hundreds of millions of dollars it behoves the government and parliament to be very sure there will not be any rip-offs in the international market at the cost of the Canadian taxpayers and the consuming public. Already there is a lot of rumour that posted international prices for oil are being undercut. It is rumoured that oil is available in some places at substantially below stated prices.
The minister must be in a position to ensure that "in between" operators are not making undue profits by gouging Canadian taxpayers and failing to give them the benefit of lower prices while, at the same time, receiving compensation at the taxpayers' expense.
There is a fundamental question here involving free enterprise and the constitutionality of what the minister proposes to do as well as what the provinces have done, and may do in the future, with respect to their natural resources. On this question I believe there is little doubt that the ownership of the oil in the ground or of other resources is vested in the provinces. I also believe there is little doubt that the provinces have complete power to legislate in respect of the oil in the ground and the royalties that they may charge. Both of those powers are clearly set out in the British North America Act. The provinces have complete power to legislate in respect of any oil rigs installations, refineries, storage tanks, pipe lines, etc. within the provinces, again by virtue of the British North America Act.
As the minister knows, these powers given to any province are subject to Ottawa's sanction, perhaps by having the Lieutenant Governor refuse his consent. But what is most disturbing is the fact that both the dominion authority and the provincial authorities have power to tax. For example, a province has the right to levy direct taxation within the province in order to raise revenue for provincial purposes; that is provided by section 92(2) of the British North America Act. But the parliament of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction over the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation; that is provided by section 91(3).
It is readily apparent that in this situation two legislatures are dealing with the same matter, namely, revenue earned by those who produce oil, in the case under debate, or for that matter those who produce gas or any other natural resource in Canada. Surely it is wrong for the federal government to persist in a course of confrontation. That fact is that taxation both at the provincial and at the federal level could take more than 100 per cent of the total revenue earned in the primary resource field if the two legislatures saw fit.
In this respect I would point out that we in Ontario are very familiar with a case that was heard in 1909 in our Supreme Court, confirmed in the Court of Appeal and eventually in the Privy Council, a case that dealt specifically with the power of the legislature virtually to confiscate private property. In that case, known as Forence Mining Co., Limited v. Cobalt Lake Mining Co., Limited, Mr. 
Justice Riddell made the position very clear when he said the following:
In short, the Legislature within its jurisdiction can do everything that is not naturally impossible, and is restrained by no rule human or divine. If it be that the plaintiffs acquired any rights, which I am far from finding, the Legislature had the power to take them away. The prohibition, "Thou slialt not steal," has no legal force upon the sovereign body. And there would be no necessity for compensation to be given. We have no such restriction upon the power of the Legislature as is found in some States.
Clearly, then, we are in a position where, if Ottawa persists in one course with respect to taxation, and the provinces persist in another course, there could be confiscation of all the earnings of the companies involved in producing natural resources.
The reason we in Ontario are concerned about this is that we believe, as I have indicated, that the first priority we must insist upon is security of supply. Surely it behooves this government and the provincial governments in the oil producing provinces to come to an agreement on the mode of taxation so that developers and resource companies can ensure we have sufficient resources in future years to enable Ontario and the rest of the country to continue their productivity without letup.
In this respect I think it is very easy for us to deal in figures of $6.50 per barrel, or $10 per barrel, or $8 per barrel, without realizing that as one of the main consumers the province of Ontario will be done irreparable harm unless there is a satisfactory reconciliation between the oil producing provinces and the federal government. Already the effects of the recent price increases are being felt dramatically in Ontario in terms of inflation and employment. I urge the members of this House to press the government to reconcile this question quickly, and on a satisfactory basis, so there is a minimum of consternation in the coming months.
In this regard I believe that the bill should be dealt with in committee of the whole so as to give ample opportunity to all members of the House to question the minister and his officials on any aspect of the bill about which they feel concern. Perhaps in this way we can get to the facts and satisfy ourselves that in truth the federal government is making an earnest attempt to satisfy all parties. Thus the Canadian consumer-and I speak as a resident of Ontario-will suffer minimum hardship.
In conclusion, I believe insufficient discussion has been conducted between the provinces and the federal government on this issue. I believe it is wrong for the government to assume that an agreement which was originally for a period of 15 months should now be embodied in an act of parliament without further consultation with the provinces to ensure that this is their wish. We are dealing with perhaps one of the most important subjects to come before this session of parliament. I hope all members will take a deep interest in it, that the government will stop being so bull-headed and will try and work out an agreement that is mutually satisfactory both to the producing and to the consuming provinces.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are again debating a bill that had a trial run in the last parliament and is now before the House with the addition of some clauses. At this stage I think it is wise that we, as
November 4, 1974

a nation, take a look at our oil and gas position, and at the prospects not simply for the immediate future but for some years ahead. Perhaps this will be the last time this question can be debated in the House, unless it can be raised again when we are debating PetroCan.
It seems to me that this bill perpetuates a very comfortable, but short-sighted, situation. We are keeping our oil prices low for the next two or three years and encouraging consumption, while at the same time discouraging exploration and development of other oil and gas fields. As a result there is a movement of drilling rigs out of Canada. While the United States is increasing its exploration activity and its financing of oil and gas development, we in turn are decreasing our activity. As I say, we are encouraging consumption by keeping the price of our gas and oil below the world price.
At the same time the government is attempting to create one uniform price all across Canada. This poses great problems, and as oil and energy are interchangeable and can be replaced with electricity, coal, wood and other forms of energy, we are not allowing the market price to set priorities. Thus we will end up with abnormal strains in the industrial and financial part of our economy when we finally must reach world market levels.
Again this bill is a direct intervention in provincial affairs in that it attempts to wrest from the provinces the right to control their resources and sell them at the best prices available. The thrust of this bill is interesting in that it intends to pillory the western provinces in favour of central Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has carefully prepared the way by appointing to the supreme court individuals who are biased against the provinces, and particularly western Canada.
What about energy savings? At a time when the world is saving energy Canada has the enviable or disreputable distinction, whatever you would call it, of experiencing an increase in the use of gas oil in the 1970's. Contrast this with the United States which has enormous natural energy supplies which in the long run will likely be cheaper than ours.
President Ford indicated in Washington that if his voluntary energy conservation program is unsuccessful he will take stronger action. He wants to have one-million barrels a day reduction in oil imports to the United States, and has said that he will move to any other alternative, including the possibility of mandatory limitations to achieve that result. This clearly indicates what lies ahead for U.S. consumers. The public is being given a chance to find its own way to conserve energy.
Voluntary programs of this type have a poor record of success. When they are judged to be failures there will no doubt already be a reduced availability of gas at the service pump, and this will be followed by the introduction of a system of priorities in respect of access to supplies, perhaps with tax devices designed to discourage heavy consumption.
To this government and Canadians generally who are enjoying temporary easing of oil prices because of ample supplies, the United States problem may seem remote. Canadians are fond of telling themselves that, on balance,
Oil and Petroleum
their country is self-sufficient in oil. This complacent attitude could lead to difficulty within three or four years and, unless Canadians think seriously about energy conservation, mandatory limitations such as those threatened by President Ford may have to be introduced in Canada.
The president of Shell Canada Limited has said that the production of crude oil and natural gas liquids from known reserves in Canada will begin to decline by about 1978, just four years from now. He also stated that if the demand continues to increase at its present rate Canada could become a net importer of oil before 1978. He went on to say that in the short term there is not much that can be done to increase supply.
The president of Shell also noted that the rate of growth in the demand for all types of energy in Canada increased from 4 per cent per annum in the 1950's to 5.5 per cent in the 1960's. As we become more mobile, more electrical and more automatic we become more energy inefficient. Most observers feel that in the long term, given significant development of the oil sands and of reserves in the frontier regions, Canada should be able to remain essentially self-sufficient in oil and natural gas, providing we espouse a conservative ethic now.
Conservation to many authorities means reducing the consumption of oil and gas liquids from the recent annual growth rate of 5.5 per cent to 6 per cent back to the 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent of the 1950's. This should not mean a change in the lifestyle of Canadians. Nor will it mean an absolute decline in consumption. However, when we are debating such things as an open-door policy on immigration, through which we could have a flood of immigrants who would certainly increase demand on energy resources, we must remember that this could well pose severe strains on our energy resources.
This change in lifestyle has been studied in the United States. The Ford Foundation has released the results of its $4 million energy policy project. The Mobil Oil Corporation criticized the low or zero growth recommendations contained in that report. We are now debating whether we should substitute small cars for large cars, how we should heat our houses in the winter and how we should cool them in the summer. I think it is often forgotten that one of the things that has made the lifestyle for Canadians much better in the last three decades has been the increased use of energy in heating homes and in transportation.
Transportation is the greatest area in which inefficiencies in energy use are to found. Air travel requires 10 times as much energy as buses, six times as much as trains, and four times as much as cars. Many industries could use coal instead of natural gas, yet this bill will allow natural gas to be sold indiscriminately at considerably lower than its market value.
This bill will increase the tendency for increased consumption of oil and natural gas, because those energy sources will continue to be priced below the world market. There is no valid argument against the suggestion that in a country such as this, with relative sufficiency, we can prevent unnecessary hardship to our consumers. However, there is no use burying our head in the sand, as this bill would imply, by saying there will be a gradual rise in oil prices to meet the world level. It should be made obvious

November 4, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
that there must be a gradual increase in oil prices to the consumer to somewhere near the world level, and we should be given details as to when this will occur.
Let me turn for a moment to what our energy possibilities are in the short run. When Premier Lougheed, the premier of Alberta, Canada's major oil producing province, after meeting with the Prime Minister stated that he was apprehensive of an energy shortage in Canada in a decade, I believe that his comments should be taken with considerable importance. Other people in the oil industry are forecasting that oil production could start to decline at the end of this decade. It has been widely quoted that on the latest data regarding performance of oil fields operating at peak levels-and this has been the case for the last one and a half years-the outlook is even more sobering.
By 1983 it is likely that Canadian production will be able to supply only Canadian areas it has served traditionally, that is, west of the Ottawa Valley. This would be of great significance in terms of Canada's balance of payments. It seems likely that by 1983 or 1984 this could account for a deficit of several billions of dollars.
It is also considered that by the latter half of the 1980's production from Canadian sources will again be more than enough to supply the traditional domestic market. It is widely considered that even if exports stop, the peak provision capacity will only be increased by three or four years. To cut off exports we would have to balance the effect on foreign exchange and on over-all foreign relations between the United States and Canada, as well as the effect on the income of producing provinces through the service industries. We would have to take into account the fact that exports generate cash for future development.
We in this country have been lulled into a feeling that the oil sands will provide unlimited supplies of cheap energy, but all indications are that this recovery of oil will be slow. One plant capable of 100,000 barrels per day capacity in the tar sands, coming on stream every two years, is considered to be all that can be expected. One oil company president has stated that it is doubtful if more than one major plant can be built in the Athabasca oil sands every two years.
A major plant now under construction is intended to start producing 125,000 barrels a day of synthetic crude in 1977. The president of that company stated that the one clear signal to the consumer that the days are over when energy supply can be taken for granted would be if we were to allow the price of petroleum and of other forms of energy to find their proper market value.
There has been a widespread feeling that oil companies have been making too much money or too high a percentage of profit. Surely it would be better to devise a means of taxing profits when prices rise, particularly if they are too high in the present situation, in order to keep the price down as a means of limiting company profits.
We are now debating whether we should extend the Montreal pipeline. In my opinion this is one move that we should not make at this time. Obviously Interprovincial Pipeline is not happy with the possibility of building that pipeline. Indeed Interprovincial seems to feel that it needs further government guarantees before it will embark on

the project. Apparently the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has stated publicly he believes in an adjustment in the tariff for all customers along the Interprovincial pipeline from Edmonton to Toronto and Montreal, and that in the end-it would be a better way to build a pipeline with an additional capacity of 250,000 barrels a day whether or not oil is available to the pipeline. In other words, those involved in the oil industry are not really sure there will be any oil to place in the pipeline even if it should be built.
This extension of the line to Montreal, which market is now served by foreign crude, is central to the policy of self-sufficiency announced after the oil embargo. Montreal obtains its oil mostly from Venezuela, while the Maritimes are served by the Middle East. A capacity of 250,000 barrels a day would fall far short of the requirements to meet eastern needs.
A more important consideration is that Interprovincial clearly has doubt concerning the availability of oil for a period of 20 years. Interprovincial raises the point whether the limits on resources are now becoming clearly visible.
What about the tar sands? Shell Explorer, the Canadian subsidiary of American Shell, wants out in respect of its half of the Shell Canada tar sands development because it doubts it can achieve an acceptable rate of return for the $500 million it would have to invest. The doubt arises from the expanding government control over the petroleum industry, which emerges from different events such as the federal-provincial tax conflict and the adoption of a policy of self-sufficiency.
It might seem to those people who want Canadians to own the oil industry that here would be an excellent opportunity for Shell Explorer to sell its share to some Canadian company, but an amount of $500 million is no mean investment for Canada at this time.
There have been frequent headlines in the papers in connection with this situation. These headlines point out, for instance, that droves of drilling rigs are leaving. This emphasizes what has been happening in respect of the exploration industry. Drilling activity has been reported at 10 per cent below the 1973 level, with the sharpest reduction in Saskatchewan, at a time when it should be expanding. As well, production in Saskatchewan has gone down by 73,000 barrels a day from a year ago. Mr. J. G. Wotherspoon, Saskatchewan Deputy Minister of Mines, stated that medium crude has been priced out of the American market. It was the export tax that priced it out, Mr. Speaker.
Alberta production is down 200,000 barrels. This reduction has come about because of the disinclination of Americans to pay the export tax in total. Unfortunately it has had its heaviest effects on the types of crude that we have in the greatest quantity, the heavy oils of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The question of the Montreal pipeline should be looked at again. Last winter the industry found it could move one-quarter million barrels a day into eastern Canada via the Panama Canal and by the Great Lakes. We might well consider this for the future. I think the security offered by this route is adequate. Indeed, instead of spending all this

money on an interprovincial pipeline the money could be spent for the development of reserves in the Alberta tar sands, and the pipeline could be proceeded with later if there should be any oil to fill it.
What are the chances of the world price of oil being reduced in the next few years? They do not seem very great, although there are a few hopeful signs around the world. In today's paper it is reported that the Shah of Iran has said he would seek a 14 per cent cutback in oil prices, but he coupled with that statement an argument that the oil companies are making too much profit. I suspect he is only trying to cloud the issue, because the substantial part of oil profits finds its way into the coffers of some governments around the world.
Officials of the British Petroleum Company in an interview in Montreal suggested that it is clear the world can produce energy from a number of sources, beginning early in the next century, at rates as prolific as those of the energy-rich years of the 1950's and 1960's, although at substantially higher prices. They went on to say that some countries such as Canada, and Britain with its North Sea oil, could be shown on paper to be able in theory to achieve self-sufficiency in respect of energy.
But it seems likely that pressures, some of them related to resource technology as well as the resources themselves, will be such that no country should really consider itself self-sufficient. Canada is part of the North American continent, and we should not attempt to isolate ourselves from the United States in respect of energy. The natural flow is north-south in the great plains of North America with regard to gas and oil.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has flatly rejected any sharing with the United States, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has just returned from France where, among other things, he explored the possibility of expanded trade in which Canadian oil, coal and uranium could be substantial elements. I always thought these were part of the energy package. The Prime Minister no doubt wishes to break down some of the dependence of Canada on the United States market. This is not the first time a Canadian Prime Minister has wished to do this. However, the United States generally is in a position to return a greater trade advantage than could be had from Europe.
Canada at the present time does not need access to the United States market as it did previously. There are now genuine shifts in energy sources in the U.S. This, together with control of wastage and a desire to strengthen conservation measures, all combines to restrain demand. The principal strength of the United States is its capacity to organize and focus money and expertise in a manner peculiar to it.
Although the United States is now involved with conservation it will find new sources of energy. Indeed the world must find new sources if it is to exist. Canada could be the loser if it denied itself access to United States technology.
This bill does not provide any method by which the provinces can work out their taxation problems. We are awaiting with interest what this month's budget will contain in an attempt to heal the wounds of the May 6 budget.
Oil and Petroleum
In the May 6 budget the federal government obviously declared war on the provinces which were producing oil and gas. The disallowance in the budget of May 6 of the provincial tax or royalty as an expense effectively placed those resources under the federal government. In western Canada this caused a growing realization of alienation. It will strengthen the idea which is gaining ground in the west that the west should adopt a much more independent position in the Canadian federation. If the resource industry is to settle down, the federal and provincial governments must come to some agreement.
The petroleum industry of Canada has pointed out that at the new Alberta crude oil price of $6.50 per barrel, and under current royalty and tax rules, sufficient cash flows are available for an additional 77 cents per barrel investment in the search for new petroleum energy. The industry also points out that the May budget proposals would have taxed away an additional $1.30 per barrel from the Alberta oil industry. The industry would suffer a loss on Saskatchewan oil production. It is obvious that there is a need for re-examination by the federal government of its tax sharing policy so that Canada will be better able to generate the capacity necessary for resource development.
It seems that much will have to come from the reinvestment by the energy companies themselves, and this will require tax regulations which would allow for a reasonable return and, at the same time, for a contribution to over-all exploration and development. There are those who believe that governments should do the investing, but all indications are that governments tend to be inefficient and prone to overkill in their control of oil companies whose profits are proverbial. It seems to me that outright government intervention and management should not be condoned when the industry can be controlled just as well by taxation and regulation.
In closing I should like to say that this bill perpetuates a principle that is wrong in that it encourages consumption and discourages conservation, exploration and the development of new oil and gas resources in our country. In the long run this will cause serious problems.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-32, the petroleum administration measure, which is designed to impose an export charge on crude oil and natural gas to compensate the oil companies, and to regulate the price of oil and natural gas.
Listening to the comments of some of my friends in the Conservative and Liberal Parties it seemed to me that the old adage of "play it again, Sam" it put into practice because in the last parliament, the twenty-ninth parliament, we dealt with many of the same issues in what was then Bill C-18. The problem of energy in Canada has not gone away, is still with us, and it stands as a testimonial to the failure of the Liberal and Conservative federal governments to design a national energy policy to benefit Canadians.
I think it is important that in our discussion and analysis of this bill we turn our attention to what should be the components of a national energy policy. I should like

November 4, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
to outline what we in the NDP believe are some of the essential elements in such a policy. First and foremost, we must come to grips with the issue of control of the petroleum industry in this country. For far too long we have welcomed with open arms, and without any real consideration of the long term implications, the multinational oil companies coming into Canada to develop our energy resources. As a result of that lack of forward looking policy in terms of what it means to Canadian control, we now find that 91 per cent of the oil industry here is foreign dominated. With respect to oil refining, foreign domination reaches 99 per cent. Is it any wonder then that there is a lack of a national policy that would benefit Canadians, and that instead the benefits are going to the multinational oil companies, most of which are based in the United States?
Let us look for a moment at what has been the policy of the multinational oil companies. First, their policy has been to export Canadian oil to the United States, and the more they can export, the higher are their profits. So it has been traditional in this country for us to get as much oil as possible out of the ground and to give it to the United States as quickly as possible. Therefore, for those oil companies the future supply of oil for Canadian needs has always been of secondary importance.
The second result of this lack of control over the industry by Canadians has meant that multinational oil companies have tried to charge the highest price possible. In other words, the cost of a barrel of oil or a gallon of gasoline is not based on the cost of production.
As the vice-president of Imperial Oil said last year in testimony before the Nova Scotia government, it is the policy of the oil companies to charge what the market will bear. When we analyse this-and the Americans have done this-we find that it costs the American oil companies, if my memory serves me correctly, about 6 cents to produce a gallon of gasoline. In other words, the idea is that the sky is the limit, and what you can get away with is perfectly all right so far as price is concerned.
The other element or trend in our energy policy here, because it is controlled by the multinationals, has been the movement toward a continental energy policy whereby Canada would continue to be the supplier of the raw material, and would ship it to the United States where it would be processed and manufactured into other products. So long as the policy continues that we must export our raw materials, of course we are exporting jobs, because where the jobs are created is where the raw materials are further processed and manufactured. Historically that has taken place outside this country.
Therefore it is the belief of the NDP that it is important to reserve this trend of the foreign domination of our oil industry, and to do that we propose a number of steps. The first is to have a national petroleum company. During the minority parliament we pressured the Liberal government as best we could to move in that direction, and indeed the minister does have a bill on the books. When you look at the bill for the creation of a national petroleum company you find that it looks pretty good on paper, but the question is: will all the powers in theory allocated to that company be in fact used?

What we want to see is a national petroleum company that will enter into all phases of the industry, into the exploration, the development and the refining of petroleum products. I do not have visions of people such as the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) managing such a company. Obviously we would go where the expertise is, we would contract out to those with such expertise. But the point is, if we had a truly national petroleum company-

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext: How about multinational managers?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
No, but we could contract out to Canadian well drilling companies, of which the hon. member from Calgary is one of the leaders. We would have a national petroleum company which, by getting involved in the oil market in Canada, could be a pace setter with regard to price, exploration and pipeline policy in this country. I think that is an essential first step.
This national petroleum company could also serve another very useful function, in view of the fact that we in eastern Canada are still dependent on imported oil. This company could buy oil directly and sell it directly to foreign governments, thus avoiding the multinationals and all the rip off in fees and profits that that entails. In other words, a national petroleum company Canadian owned and directed could strike the best deal for Canadians in terms of buying and selling oil.
It is very interesting to note the current wprld situation, Mr. Speaker. A few days ago in the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) admitted that in effect Canada can be blackmailed by foreign governments that have multinational head offices within their jurisdiction. We were discussing a proposed international oil agreement when this little tidbit of information came out, Mr. Speaker. This seems to me a frightful admission of a lack of Canadian sovereignty in an area vital to the survival of our economy. A national petroleum company would be the beginning of control of the industry; it would lessen and eventually end the domination and threat of blackmail by multinational oil companies.
It would be important to have a national petroleum company deal directly with foreign governments, especially oil producing governments, in light of what is taking place in the Middle East at the present time. We read in this morning's paper that the Shah of Iran is seeking a 14 per cent reduction in the posted oil price. He pointed out, however, because of our present dependence on the multinational oil companies, that there is no guarantee that the reduction would be passed on to the consumer.
Saudi Arabia has proposed a plan that would make crude oil cheaper for a national petroleum company dealing on a bilateral basis with that country and other oil producing states.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that to even the most rabid capitalist the concept of a national petroleum comapny has some merit in our present situation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
No way!
November 4, 1974

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I hear some noes from my friends on my right, so there are still a few diehards there. They are to be commended on their principles and sincerity, but they are still living in the nineteenth century. We do not have the free market that they assume we have still.
If we are to have a national energy policy, Mr. Speaker, we can no longer allow Canada to remain at the mercy of the pricing and supply policies of the multinational oil companies. We must move toward government control and ownership, and view all forms of energy as we view electricity now-a public utility. We cannot allow wasteful private competition in the energy field.
The second essential element to a national energy policy is to ensure security of supply. At the present time in Canada we are self-sufficient in oil, but because of past Conservative and Liberal government policies we do not have an oil pipeline to eastern Canada from the western oil fields. As a result eastern Canada has to import oil and consequently the country has been caught in the tremendous inflationary spiral caused by the crude oil crisis.
We are faced with some frightening prospects in the near future, Mr. Speaker. Canada currently produces
2,003,000	barrels of crude oil per day. In Canada 1,751,000 barrels a day are consumed, and 1,206,000 barrels per day are exported. We import 949,000 barrels per day. I studied oil company figures, independent studies and National Energy Board figures. We do not have the latest report of the National Energy Board, which is a shame, and I think the minister is concerned about that as well.
The latest predictions of oil availability and demand, however, indicate that Canada will no longer be self-sufficient by 1979-only five years away. Canada's oil production is declining, yet we are still exporting oil to the United States at an incredible rate because of a lack of government intervention and because of foreign domination of the industry.
At the same time that oil production in western Canada is declining, demand is increasing rapidly. Any sane, logical person must ask why we continue to export oil when predictions are that we are running short and will have to import more expensive oil from Venezuela and the Arab states.
There are many answers, Mr. Speaker. In the past the National Energy Board consistently has been over-optimistic about future supply. It has accepted oil company figures, and it is to the advantage of the oil companies to be optimistic about supply in order to encourage exports. There is no pipeline to eastern Canada as an alternative to the demand of the United States market, and consequently the exports go to the United States. There has been consistent pressure on the Canadian government and the National Energy Board from multinational companies to commit ourselves to exporting oil.
Another reason why we do not cut back on exports to the United States is that since we have had the current world crisis and the price has gone up, the Canadian government has become dependent on revenues generated by the export tax to compensate consumers in eastern Canada in order to keep their oil price below the high world level. The policy of continuing to export under these circumstances is self-defeating as we run short of domes-
Oil and Petroleum
tic oil. Exports will decline, export tax revenues will decline, and meanwhile the demand for imported oil in eastern Canada will continue to increase. Where is the money to come from to compensate the oil companies and to keep the Canadian price lower than the world price?
The government has two options, Mr. Speaker. First, in the years ahead it can compensate the oil companies from general tax revenues. That means each and every Canadian will have to pay more in taxes in order to have a lower price in Canada than the world price. Or secondly, the government will have to let the price of oil in Canada rise to world levels.
The implications are astounding in terms of what that would do to inflation in this country. Every day our constituents complain about increases in the cost of food, clothing and other essential items, but if we were to let the price of Canadian oil rise to world levels they would see what inflation really means. Energy is the essential component to our total economy; if energy costs go up so do costs in every other area.
When we look at demand and production in this country, the future is not promising. In 1979 we will lose our self-sufficiency. In effect, we will be in a deficit position of 101,000 barrels per day, and by 1984-a year that has some other connotations-we will be in a deficit position of 970,000 barrels per day, and will have to import oil from the Arab states and Venezuela at a higher price.
Given this evidence, that we are losing production in the west and demand is going up, it seems to me imperative to begin to reduce substantially exports to the United States. The minister says the government is considering this, and that it may be a possibility. He is admitting that it may be in Canada's interest to cut back somewhat our oil exports.
I remind the House that the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works has another item before it. It is called an international oil agreement, and is an agreement between 11 consuming countries, of which Canada is to be a member. This international oil agreement is a 10 year treaty. It is important to note that in this treaty the United States has a voting mandate of 53 votes and Canada only has a voting mandate of nine votes.
Under the terms of this treaty, which the Canadian government seems ready to ratify, if an international oil emergency develops, that is, if there is a shortage in any of the 11 importing countries, Canada is then committed to continue exporting oil to the United States at its current rate of export.
The implications of this agreement are indeed serious if we are determined to cut back our oil exports to the United States. If we get into an emergency situation, Canada will lose control of cutting back exports to the United States. Conceivably, Canadians would have to undergo cutbacks and rationing to serve the U.S. market. We need to take a closer look at this proposed international oil agreement. I looks like the beginning of a continental oil policy.
In terms of security of supply, in addition to cutting back exports to the United States it is essential that we begin to build an all-Canadian pipeline to eastern Canada.

November 4, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
This pipeline should go from Manitoba through northern Ontario to Montreal and the maritimes. I advocated this on many occasions in the last parliament. The answer the minister gave me on why we could not build an all Canadian line was that it would take a year extra to complete over the proposed Sarnia-Montreal pipeline. We now have delays in the Sarnia-Montreal pipeline to the point that these delays equal the one year extra it would have taken to build an all Canadian route.
I also argued with the minister in the last parliament about the value of a Sarnia-Montreal pipeline as opposed to extending the existing pipeline from Toronto to Montreal. The minister argued we needed the Sarnia pipeline because it could carry 500,000 barrels a day. Now that pipeline is supposed to carry only 300,000 barrels a day, and Interprovincial is not even sure it can handle that. With an all Canadian pipeline, we would have the opportunity to open up a petrochemical industry in northern Ontario. More important, we would have a means of getting cheaper western Canadian oil to our eastern market, and we would be secure in knowing that it traversed only through Canadian territory. This again raises the issue of security.
I am astounded to realize that the Canadian government is now negotiating with the United States about the security of supply through pipelines. I always assumed we had a treaty with the United States guaranteeing security of supply for the pipeline that leaves western Canada via Alberta and Manitoba, goes to Chicago, and links up with Sarnia again. There is also a pipeline from Portland, Maine, to Montreal.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources now tells us we are negotiating with the United States for guaranteed security. Meanwhile, what do the Americans want? They want an oil pipeline and gas pipeline through the Mackenzie Valley. The implications are serious.
Our pipelines going through American territory are not secure. The Americans are in a tremendous bargaining position to argue they should have a pipeline down the Mackenzie. It really amounts to blackmail. An all Canadian route would certainly avoid that difficulty.
If we are to have guaranteed future supply we must begin to develop the Athabasca oil sands. We must do this on a concerted and energetic basis. In the last parliament the minister repeatedly said the Athabasca oil sands were the great salvation of Canada. It was a secure supply. We had to develop the plants, get them on stream and into production because of the time lag involved. I do not hear the minister touting the Athabasca oil sands as the great salvation any longer. It is important that we understand why there is this sudden silence.
Here is a golden opportunity for Canada to move toward self sufficiency. We have an opportunity at this time due to the fact that in one of the proposed developments of the oil sands one of the private multinational companies is pulling out. Here is an excellent change for a government national petroleum company to step in as one of the partners to develop the oil sands under Canadian terms, for the benefit of Canadians and not for the export markets in the United States.

In the last parliament we asked for a 50/50 split of the export tax between the provinces and the federal government so that the provinces could have extra revenue to help develop, along with the federal government, energy projects such as the oil sands. This was not accepted. Under the current export tax there is a surplus of some $200 million this year. I wonder what the federal government will do with that surplus. Is it going to turn it back into energy development? It is important that we have answers to these questions.
Another way we can begin to move toward ensuring a supply of oil for future Canadians is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources seriously to advocate to Canadians the value of conservation of energy. I do not mean turning out the lights around Parliament Hill. We have to get Canadians to think conservation because, as I said, we are moving toward a lack of self-sufficiency within five years time.
It is interesting to note that the growth in demand for energy in Canada during the 1950's was 4 per cent per annum. By the 60's, the demand had grown to 5.5 per cent. Canadians consume energy at a rate five times higher than the world average.
This government has a responsibility to initiate energy saving policies in areas such as higher insulation standards for new homes. We need to encourage mass transit via bus and train. In terms of passenger miles, planes require 10 times as much fuel as buses, six times as much fuel as trains, and four times as much fuel as cars. Yet the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is going full speed ahead with STOL, the short takeoff and landing aircraft. He should be putting more money into mass transit via train and bus.
To promote conservation the federal government should be urging the provinces to reduce highway speed limits to 50 miles an hour. A car uses between 15 and 25 per cent more gasoline at 70 miles an hour than at 50.
If the minister had the courage to urge Canadians to turn down their thermostats four degrees, we would save the equivalent of 900 million gallons of fuel oil a year, about 10 per cent of the energy used in heating. We should also begin to phase out the use of natural gas to produce electricity because it is so inefficient when used that way. Further we should discourage the use of electricity to heat homes because more energy is expended in producing electricity than is warranted when we consider the ratio of electricity needed to heat homes. Those are some positive steps the government could take to move toward a position of security in future oil supplies.
A third element of a national energy policy surely must be a pricing policy to benefit Canadians. In the last parliament, and even before, the New Democratic Party advocated a two-price system in oil. That is to say, Canadians would pay a lower price than the world price, and we would export our oil at the higher world price. As a result of that policy which was accepted in the last parliament, Canadians save approximately $5.20 a barrel for crude oil. However, we still got caught in an increase of sorts because the price of oil to the Canadian consumer had to go up in eastern Canada because there was no pipeline from the west. We had to import foreign oil.

To keep the price down to consumers the government said it would absorb the difference in price between what people were paying in eastern Canada, the world price, and what people were paying in western Canada, the Canadian price. The money would in turn be given to companies operating in eastern Canada to keep the price down.
To date the government has given some $900 million to the oil companies in compensation payments. I maintain this is a rip-off of the Canadian consumer when we consider what company profits have amounted to this year. It seems to me, in the light of these profits, that the companies could well afford to absorb a greater share of the increased cost of the oil imported into eastern Canada.
Let me give the House a few examples of oil company profits. The after tax profits of Gulf Oil in 1972 amounted to $64.2 million. In 1973 profits rose to $101.7 million, an increase of 58 per cent. In 1972 the profits of Imperial Oil amounted to $157 million. By 1973 they had risen to $228 million, an increase of 45 per cent.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext: That is a return on capital investment.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Moreover, for nine months since 1973, Imperial Oil profits have shown a further increase of 64 per cent. The figures for Shell this year are equally remarkable. In 1973 Shell showed a profit of $60 million; in 1974 the figure is $119.5 million, an increase of almost 100 per cent. Yet we are giving $900 million a year to these oil companies!
Even more striking than figures I have just quoted are some figures here which, so far, have not been brought out in this debate. They show the profits of these companies as a percentage of revenue. With respect to Gulf Oil, profit as a percentage of revenue in 1969 was 6.8 per cent. By 1973 the figure had risen to 9.6 per cent. For Imperial Oil in 1969 the figure was 6.2 per cent; in 1973 it was 8.6 per cent. This means that despite the export tax, despite the corporate income tax, our tax system is still allowing the oil companies to keep a larger proportion of their revenue. I argue that the oil companies cannot plead that they lack funds for exploration. They are very healthy indeed, healthy enough, in my opinion, to absorb some of the higher costs of imported crude.
In conclusion may I repeat that Canada is approaching an energy shortage which will become evident in four or five years. A serious crisis is coming and we, as members of parliament, must bear the responsibility to act in a meaningful, constructive and responsible way to meet this crisis. We must develop a national energy policy embodying public control to achieve three things: Canadian control of the oil industry, security of supply, and fair prices for Canadians along the lines I and my party have suggested.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I had not intended to take part in this debate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Oh, come on!
Oil and Petroleum,

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The bill is a good one and I think it is necessary. As the last speaker mentioned, we have been over this ground again and again. I sometimes wonder, though, whether members of the opposition have ever taken time to read the bill and, if so, whether they have come to any conclusions about it.
Perhaps it would be useful if I were to remind hon. members that it concerns a charge levied on the export of crude oil and certain petroleum products to provide compensation for certain petroleum costs, and to regulate the price of Canadian crude and natural gas in interprovincial and export trade.
I have been waiting to hear from hon. members opposite either support for this proposition or opposition to it. Instead, I hear the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) telling us there is no point, now, in building the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal. Five minutes later the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) tells us that not only should it be built but that it should be reversible so that should the price of offshore crude go down, or supplies be found off the east coast, we might be in a good position to take advantage of these circumstances. So, we hear two differing points of view.
From the New Democratic Party we hear speakers hashing over the idea of an all Canadian pipeline to meet an emergency situation. Is it any wonder that the government must show leadership and bring forward a bill which speaks, not for Alberta or for Ontario, but for Canada? I listened to the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), and I listened to the usual harangue by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) that royalties should be allowed as an expense of doing business. However, neither of them indicated what amount of royalty they thought was reasonable.
When the price was frozen at $4.00 a barrel, the provinces and the federal government got together and arrived at a figure of $6.50 a barrel which was felt to be in the common interest of Canada. It was a little less than Alberta wanted for its crude, and it was a little more than Ontario wanted to pay, but it was a compromise worked out to deal with the situation. What was the reaction of the provinces? Saskatchewan felt that the oil companies did not need the extra money and decided to take the whole of the $2.50 increase. Alberta, if I am not mistaken, took between 65 and 70 per cent.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated prior to his meetings with the Premiers of the western provinces that they should not try to take all of that increase and call it a royalty, and that if they did it would not be allowed as an expense of doing business. This was a reasonable position for the Prime Minister to take. He stated it early on so that the provinces would be aware of the federal government's position. Fortunately we had the strength to maintain that position, and when the producing provinces took the action they did, the federal government had no alternative but to say that it is not a royalty, that this is a total intrusion into another tax field, and it is not a legitimate royalty to be allowed as an expense of doing business.
Negotiations now have to take place to determine what, in effect, is a reasonable royalty. I make no secret of the

November 4, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
fact-indeed, I spoke about this publicly during the campaign-that the oil companies should be allowed a reasonable royalty as an expense of doing business. Whether or not such a compromise can be worked out I do not know, but at this point in time to suggest that $2.50 of an increase, or 65 or 70 per cent, should be the royalty, is begging the question. That is why the federal government took the action it had to take.
Once again we have the selective memory of the opposition parties when they say the government has been lacking in leadership. I suggest they are really choking on that particular expression. They tend to forget that the price of oil per barrel in the world was quadrupled and, as a result, we had to meet an emergency situation. We did this in several ways. We did it by delivering the oil in a way which the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) said was so successful that he wanted it adopted as a permanent way of moving oil from the west to the east, namely, by ship, train and any other way. So that operation must have been comparatively successful, Mr. Speaker.
The position of the federal government is that we want a one-price system for oil in Canada, give or take a few cents to allow for transportation costs. Is the opposition suggesting that this is inappropriate? If it is, then hon. members opposite should stand up and say so. It seems to us that having a two-price system is a good move. We should have one price across Canada within the limits that I have indicated, and then impose an export tax, which is a legitimate tax, on oil we ship outside. This money would not be used to fill the government's coffers.
There is a surplus of $200 million now, but I have not heard any member say how that money should be spent. They view it with suspicion, and wonder what the federal government is going to do with it. Surely these members have an obligation either to say they approve or they disapprove on the second reading of this bill, which is approval in principle.
Then I hear opposition members harping on the fact that the minister suggested that one option open on the Mont-real-Sarnia pipe line was that, in order to pay for the capital cost of the line, a flow through charge should be made to users. With respect, that is one option that must be considered. Another option is that Interprovincial Pipe Line go ahead and build the pipe line as they were going to in the first place. Another is that they get a guarantee of a flow through charge, with the federal government picking up any shortfall in amount. Yet another option is that the federal government build the pipe line, or that the federal government build the pipe line and sell it back to Interprovincial. There is a whole series of options which surely must be examined.
Much has been made of the fact that we were confronted with an emergency situation, yet construction of the pipe line has been delayed. It has been held up because the National Energy Board saw its responsibility. It knew this was an emergency situation, and it also knew that there was apprehension in the province of Quebec about environmental damage. So the board told Interprovincial Pipe Line to find another route, that it did not feel it could approve the present route. As I say, the National Energy Board saw its responsibility and had the courage and good sense to do what it did. Surely it has a responsibility to

tell provincial pipe line companies where to build their pipe lines so there is as little impact on the environment as possible.
I suggest to the hon. member for Calgary Centre that the most ridiculous suggestion I have heard tonight in this debate is that we should withdraw clause 36. Somewhere down the line the federal government has to take its responsibility. It is endeavouring to negotiate, for the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta, a price for their oil. If this cannot be negotiated, would not the opposition be justified in saying to the government that it has reached the stage where it cannot come to any kind of settlement, so why not introduce legislation to set the price?
This bill does not set a price unilaterally. There are all kinds of opportunities, both for the consuming and the producing provinces, to negotiate a reasonable price. But if this cannot be done surely the federal government must take its responsibility.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has given us a studious commentary on Bill C-32. The areas of this bill with which I agree are already clearly on the record, and they have been placed there by other members of my party. Similarly, other members of my party have clearly defined their areas of stern disapproval. Those areas of disapproval were voiced a moment ago by the previous member who was quick to praise clause 36, to which I should like to come in due course.
Let me for a moment, however, examine the closing statements of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He stated that the objectives which the bill seeks to achieve are, for the most part, familiar to mem-
November 4, 1974

bers as being now well established components of an integrated national energy policy. That is an interesting statement in itself. It is very cleverly worded. You cannot really tell whether the statement means "we had an energy policy", "we have an energy policy", or "we will have an energy policy".
The question of energy policy is a very interesting one and was the subject of much remark in 1972. In fact I can remember Doug Stewart, the former member for Okanagan Kootenay, speaking about the lack of a Liberal energy policy at that time. I wonder if that is why he decided to retire. In any event the stand of the leader of my party on an energy policy was very clear in 1972: he expressed the need for the development of an energy policy, a policy that did not exist at that time, and which really does not exist today.
Let us look twice or three times at this statement, and let us look at it for what it says, not for what it purports to say. Purporting to speak of energy as oil and gas, and only oil and gas, what it really talks about, in my view, is all sources of energy, be they oil and gas, thermp nuclear, water and its hydro electric end result, or coal and coke fired steam generators. These last two, coal and coke, as well as hydro electric energy, are of considerable interest to me and of concern to my constituents. They are also of concern to the people of the riding of Okanagan Boundary. I mention that riding because of the massive coal deposits which exist in Fernie and the Crowsnest area.
Why are the people of Kootenay West concerned? I do not think there are many senior members in this House, along with the people of my riding, who will have forgotten the Columbia River sellout, the Kootenay Canal with which we are now faced, the Kootenay dams, the Libby Dam with which we have been cursed, and the massive effect on the environment at Kootenay Lake and the Pend d'Orielle River. What is the reaction of the people in my riding to that of playing waterboy to the North American continent? I think it is viewed as a threat to the people that they will be blessed with another damned dam. They have had dams up to their necks.
What are these people doing about the situation? Let us look at the record of B.C. hydro and its proposal to put a dam on the Pend d'Orielle River. The people of Trail and Fruitvale and the surrounding area were sufficiently sensible to do their homework, and they succeeded in bringing that project to a halt until proper studies had been completed on the environmental, hydro electric needs, the end results and so on. I can assure you that the concerns of the people will still be directed in that way, whether it involves hydro electricity or coal.
When the minister addresses himself to a national energy policy I frankly do not know whether he speaks of an oil and gas policy or a truly national energy policy, and I am not sure what are the parameters of such a policy. I do not think anyone knows, except perhaps the minister.
This bill we have before us does not in fact speak for Canada but speaks for an arrogant, self-centred and dictatorial administration. For the record let me again quote from Section 109 of the British North America Act. It states:
Oil and Petroleum
All lands, mines, minerals, and royalties belonging to the several Provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at the Union, and all sums then due or payable for such lands, mines, minerals, or royalties, shall belong to the several Provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick in which the same are situated or arise-
As the last speaker said, it is true that they were dealing at that time with a time frame far removed from the present, but that does not remove the responsibility on the part of the government to sit down with the provincial first ministers and do some real hard heart to heart talking. That does not preclude the necessity of some real hard bargaining. It is not good enough to say that a particular first minister will not agree. This all requires further dialogue rather than that type of confrontation.
What are the first ministers' responses now, and what will they do in future as our national policy expands so that we get into considerations of hydro electric generation, coal and thermo nuclear generation? These things are all covered under the general term energy, and this will affect all the provinces. The federal government will be involved, but the question is how, and under what terms?
Clause 36 of this bill is one that I think will give the first ministers of the provinces a future migraine headache. This bill represents a major precedent to the next step. I suggest that the next step, apart from laying the groundwork for policy in areas of energy source, will also lay the groundwork for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) when he entertains the government and the people with his forthcoming budget address. What will he do? The odds are that he will also move into the energy and natural resource fields with future taxation which will bring into effect, again by direct confrontation with the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, the whole question of resource taxation. I suggest the groundwork for that taxation is right here in this energy bill.
One might ask why I should be concerned about this and why the people of my riding should be concerned. I am concerned because of the vast resource of minerals in the riding of Kootenay West and the riding of Okanagan Kootenay, and because of the massive taxation that has already been introduced by a shortsighted provincial government. Reference has been made during the debate on this bill to a passage by Mr. Laskin. I think it deserves repeating at this time:
The respective taxing powers of dominion and provinces may not be used by either of them to sterilize powers conferred by the other upon its functionaries or substantially to impair their status.
My concern is not with the finer technical points or the major economic points to which experienced gentlemen have referred. My concerns are the concerns of the people of my riding whom I represent. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

November 4, 1974
Adjournment Debate
